The newly named attribution and intervention stages elaborate existing components. The threshold formula revision does not establish a change to the described top-fraction pruning procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Section 2 gains separate attribution and intervention subsections, while DPO motivation moves into Appendix B and baseline/metric descriptions move into Appendix A. Expanded appendices reorganize sampling explanations, evaluation details and analyses.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redrawn, and v2 adds transfer heatmaps and adaptive-training plots. Table 1 gains model and baseline rows plus metric-direction indicators. Original ablation tables and layer histograms move into the appendices, alongside substantial new ablation, adaptive-attack and metric tables.

R1.justification: Section 3 substantially expands positioning relative to detection/filtering defenses and attribution/activation patching. It explicitly locates the contribution in using attribution to understand data versus instructions rather than introducing an entirely new intervention technique, and discusses shared context-boundary assumptions. Additional references support the new attacks, model and metrics.

T1.justification: Equation 5 revises the pruning-threshold formula from a supremum expression to an infimum expression using an indicator expectation. The DPO bound, entropy decomposition, Lemma 1 and their proofs are otherwise retained and relocated to Appendices B–D. The newly stated standard F1 formulas add explanation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central robustness and quality-preservation claims through adaptive attacks, cross-attack transfer, the Φ ablation and additional quality metrics. Evaluation code and judging prompts address important reproducibility gaps in v1. These gains outweigh localized reporting errors, including the reversed α interpretation and incorrect Table 7 baseline deltas, although those errors weaken confidence in some explanations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CachePrune. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original model evaluations, ablations, cross-attack transfer tests, adaptive attacks and additional quality metrics.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on SQuAD, HotpotQA and WildChat, alongside pruning ablations, neuron analyses and code/text attack transfer results.

results.title: CachePrune: Teaching LLMs What Not to Follow via KV-Cache Editing

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion redefine the contribution from a competitive-programming benchmark into a complementary Comp/Repo suite assessing algorithmic reasoning and software-library functionality. Claims about multi-turn degradation and dependency difficulty remain, but the claimed empirical applicability now explicitly includes repository-derived software contexts.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations distinguishing shallow reasoning from capacity demands at greater dependency depth, and algorithmic errors from repository integration errors. It replaces the competition-only limitation with source-specific ingestion limitations and discussion of specialized models and debugging loops. Figure 12 also newly explains the non-monotonic relationship between structural complexity and difficulty at the simplest structures.

D1.justification: v3 adds evaluation templates and conditional prompt rules, repository import handling and Docker execution details, sampling tables, and pipeline token/cost estimates. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without proving changes to retained experiments. The forthcoming-release promise in v1 is replaced by explicit dataset and changed code-repository links.

E1.justification: The original 5,258 Codeforces problems are retained as CodeFlowBench-Comp. v3 adds evaluated repository-derived function-generation tasks covering Basic, Cryptography, Network, System, and Visualization domains. This substantially extends coverage beyond competitive programming; DomainEval's Computation domain is explicitly excluded.

E2.justification: Table 1 changes from 13 to 19 models, adding GPT-5 variants, o3-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini-2.5/3, Claude-4/4.5, and Qwen3 models. GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Yi-Coder, and QwQ leave this main comparison. GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet remain in the DSC comparison in v3 Figure 16.

E3.justification: v1 specifies the most recent 20% of problems for testing. v3 specifies 1,000 problems, but Section 4 calls them the most recent whereas Appendix E.1 describes depth-stratified sampling. This is a reported protocol revision without establishing reruns. v3 also introduces APT evaluation and new semantic, stylistic, and five-criterion quality-assessment protocols.

E4.justification: Appendix A.6 adds cross-model description-consistency tests, solution-decomposition sensitivity checks, and human/LLM subproblem-quality validation. Error analysis expands to repository tasks and Gemini-3-Flash. Conversely, v1's IR-remediation study is removed. The original four error-case illustrations are retained in v3 Appendix F.2.

E5.justification: v3 adds a sampling-distribution chi-square test with p=0.1246 and alpha=0.05, plus a variance-motivated PD@k estimation procedure in Appendix D. Neither version specifies actual repeated-run counts, seeds, or confidence intervals for the benchmark scores; the new estimator does not establish additional runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive model, repository, APT, and validation results. Table 1 newly reports Gemini-3-flash-thinking at 48.4%/65.5% multi-turn/single-turn Pass@1 on Comp and GPT-5 at 34.7%/48.8% on Repo. Retained Comp entries such as o1-mini's 20.8%/37.8% are unchanged. v1's IR-remediation results of 16.7% and 8.3% disappear. These additions do not establish same-setting performance improvements between versions.

M1.justification: The core AST-based decomposition, dependency ordering, test capture, and iterative generation procedure remain. Appendix C.2 introduces a limited repository-specific adaptation: DomainEval reference functions and tests are used directly, omitting the solution-verification step before dependency analysis.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and results discussion are extensively rewritten. The six-stage pipeline presentation is condensed into two phases, discussion is integrated into the experiments section, and the appendices are reorganized into A–G with a contents list. Existing pipeline details and error cases remain identifiable across these moves.

P2.justification: v3 changes to a two-column layout, redraws the introductory diagrams, expands the main table into Comp/Repo panels, and adds APT, validation, and sampling tables. The turn-performance plots change from four panels to two. Dataset statistics and the expanded DSC heatmap move to the appendices, while original screenshot examples are retained.

R1.justification: v3 expands positioning through DomainEval, agile-development and code-reuse literature, and additional software-engineering benchmarks. Appendix C.1 explicitly distinguishes constructive function generation from repository maintenance tasks. Earlier discussion and citations concerning TreeInstruct, EvoCodeBench, and DS-1000 are removed, substantially revising the research context.

T1.justification: v1 defines PD(k) as the maximum observed depth over k attempts. v3 Appendix D defines an expected maximum and derives an unbiased estimator using ordered depths from n trials and combinatorial weights. This adds substantive mathematical definition and reasoning beyond the original metric description.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's competition-only limitation through evaluations on repository-derived functions across five domains, strengthening the empirical basis for its real-world-workflow claims. Pipeline validation and detailed evaluation templates also improve scrutiny and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of the IR-remediation analysis. However, conflicting sampling descriptions and an explicitly permissive quality-scoring prompt remain material weaknesses and limit confidence in some stronger interpretations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CodeFlowBench. The original benchmark is identifiable as CodeFlowBench-Comp in v3, and the complete text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original evaluations and adds repository-derived tasks, additional model results, pipeline ablations, and human/LLM quality assessments.

before.justification: v1 reports original multi-turn and single-turn model evaluations, dependency-complexity analyses, error distributions, and an IR-remediation study.

results.title: CodeFlowBench: A Multi-turn, Iterative Benchmark for Complex Code Generation

C1.justification: The automatic synthesis and human-comparable quality claims remain. However, v2 adds a central contribution that HopWeaver discovers diverse reasoning patterns exposing limitations of advanced RAG systems, and broadens its stated value to challenging benchmarks and targeted training in the abstract, introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 interprets RAG performance gaps as dependence on benchmark-specific reasoning patterns. Its error analysis acknowledges formatting effects and occasional insufficient evidence, qualifying v1's attribution to model errors. Limitations now discuss backbone/corpus dependence, inherited bias and English-only testing; the two-hop focus remains documented in Appendix B.

D1.justification: Appendix H adds concrete RAG settings, including Llama3-8B-Instruct, e5-base-v2, input length, retrieval depth and FlashRAG prompts. Appendix B newly explains benchmark question-type selection. Existing synthesis hyperparameters, hardware, cost information and code-access instructions are largely retained.

E1.justification: The English Wikipedia corpus, benchmark datasets and bridge/comparison coverage remain. Section 5.4 adds an end-to-end RAG scenario in which answers depend on retrieved context, extending the earlier separate retrieval and question-only/golden-document QA evaluations.

E2.justification: v2 Table 4 introduces a substantial new comparison involving Standard RAG, REPLUG, SuRe, FLARE and IRCoT. The comparator sets in the retained quality, retrieval and ablation experiments are unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include a separate 500-sample validation, 50 human-rated question pairs selected with LLM-score differences above 0.3, and a random 100-question reasoning-path audit. The RAG experiment introduces Llama3-8B-Instruct with a 2048-token input limit and top-five retrieval. Existing main evaluations are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds sample-size validation, human validation of the judge and manual reasoning-path assessment. It expands v1's brief GPT-4o error inspection into a quantified 49-case breakdown: 18 formatting differences, 29 reasoning errors and two insufficient-evidence cases. The original reranker and polisher ablations are retained and relocated.

E5.justification: Table 9 extends reliability reporting to human evaluation through majority/unanimous agreement and three-rater Fleiss' kappa. The existing judge-stability procedure—five independent runs at temperature zero, with SD, alpha and kappa—is unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the retained ablation results are unchanged. New results include RAG scores, dataset statistics, 500-sample quality scores and human audits. For example, Table 4 reports bridge F1 of 0.318 for Standard RAG versus 0.158 for IRCoT; Table 10 reports 92% correct reasoning paths. Table 9 reports 94% human-majority agreement, although Section 4.1 inconsistently states 92%.

M1.justification: The synthesis steps, MMR retrieval, simulated-feedback reranker, filtering and polishing procedures remain unchanged. The clarified fallback between direct recommendation and diversified search was already specified in v1's prompt appendix.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution list, conclusion and limitations are rewritten. Related work becomes Section 2, preliminaries move to Appendix A, and main-text ablations move to Appendix C. These changes substantially reorganize the narrative while retaining most method and prompt descriptions.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the tabular presentation with RAG, dataset-statistics, larger-sample, human-agreement and reasoning-path tables. Existing ablation tables move to the appendix, and table captions and floats are repositioned. The core diagrams, radar plot and reliability heatmaps are retained.

R1.justification: A new three-part Related Works section substantially expands the previously scattered positioning around datasets, synthesis and evaluation. It distinguishes rule-based, neural, structured-resource and recent LLM approaches, adding works such as Du et al. (2017), Chen et al. (2024b) and HopRAG.

T1.justification: The comparison-path definition is corrected: v1 Equation 6 begins with the self-loop (e1, r1, e1), whereas v2 Appendix A Equation 8 uses (e1, r1, e2) and consistent terminal indices. The remaining constraints, retrieval equation, loss and reliability formulas are retained.

improvement.justification: The human judge-validation study and quantified reasoning-path audit address important gaps in v1's evidence for dataset quality. Larger-sample checks and end-to-end RAG tests further strengthen validation and practical relevance. These gains substantially improve the paper, although the 92%/94% agreement inconsistency and interpretation of RAG gaps as proof of reasoning-pattern diversity remain weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HopWeaver research. All 27 pages of v1 and 31 pages of v2, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, support reliable comparison despite retitling and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds end-to-end RAG evaluation, larger-sample validation, human judgments and reasoning-path assessments.

before.justification: v1 reports original question-quality, QA, retrieval, reranker and polisher experiments, plus judge-reliability measurements in Appendix C.

results.title: HopWeaver: Cross-Document Synthesis of High-Quality and Authentic Multi-Hop Questions

C1.justification: v3's abstract, introduction, and conclusion elevate executable grounding's superiority to a central empirical contribution; v1 instead emphasizes general framework effectiveness and finds different prompts best for different extraction components. v3 also claims substantially broader regulatory coverage and emphasizes deployment without fine-tuning and recovery of long-range, non-linear dependencies.

C2.justification: v3 replaces much of the prompt interpretation with arguments about pseudo-code as a structural scaffold, equality over-merging, and abstraction-induced precision loss. It adds qualifications about P4 outperforming P5 in some dense cases. Limitations now explicitly cover quadratic pairwise scaling and omitted temporal constraints, exceptions, and probabilistic rules, while the earlier small-dataset limitation is removed.

D1.justification: v1 promises dataset release after acceptance; v3 states that both code and data are available and supplies a repository link, materially changing reported resource access. Appendices A.5–A.6 add text-quality criteria and annotation-processing explanations, and Figure 14 supplies the pseudo-code example's input. Conversely, v3 drops the explicit Macro-F1 specification. Resource availability is reported by the PDF and was not externally verified.

E1.justification: BPRF becomes BREX with substantially broader represented domains. Beyond v1's banking, healthcare, e-commerce, manufacturing, and service examples, v3 Section 3.2 explicitly includes scientific research management, administrative approvals, legal processes, and financial compliance across over 30 domains. The rule-extraction and dependency-identification tasks remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated model roster is largely replaced across all three tasks. v1's GPT-4o/o1, ERNIE, ChatGLM/GLM, Llama-3.1, Qwen2.5, QwQ, and DeepSeek-v3 comparisons give way to Gemini-2.5, GPT-5, Kimi-k2, DeepSeek-3.1/3.2-exp, and Qwen3 variants. DeepSeek-R1 remains. These changes appear in the actual result tables, not merely the references.

E3.justification: The evaluation corpus expands from 50 documents/326 rules to 409 documents/2,855 rules, and synthetic generation changes from ChatGPT-3.5 to Gemini-2.5-Pro. v3 adds rule-count and rule-pair-count stratification and evaluates the stricter atomic equality convention. Agreement assessment changes from annotating the dataset to an unspecified subset. v1 specifies Macro-F1 for classification; v3 says only F1, leaving any averaging change unresolved.

E4.justification: v3 adds dependency-type comparisons and systematic analyses of extraction performance versus rule density and dependency performance versus pair count (Figures 3–4). Appendix A.7 replaces v1's flight-booking, foreign-currency-deposit, and DeepSeek shopping analyses with leave, credit-card, and fixed-deposit cases examining equality over-merging and pseudo-code-induced spurious rules.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 4 introduces error bars and accompanying discussion of variability, whereas v1 provides point estimates and case scores without such dispersion displays. The bars' statistical meaning and calculation are unspecified. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, or significance tests; ICC and Fleiss' Kappa remain the annotation-agreement measures.

E6.justification: The experimental results are substantially replaced. v1 Tables 4–5 report P1 as best on average for NER (0.910) and P4 for logical classification (0.5947); v3 Tables 2–3 favor P5 (0.882 and 0.850). These are different corpora/model rosters, not same-setting performance changes. Dependency results, complexity findings, and case outcomes are also replaced or added. Reported ICC changes from 0.904 to 0.892 and Kappa from 0.911 to 0.901.

M1.justification: The two-stage extraction/dependency procedure and five prompting strategies remain. However, Prompt 4's demonstration changes from grouping b, c, and d into one equality rule in v1 Figure 11 to separate equality rules in v3 Figure 13, changing the extraction guidance. Pseudo-code prompting already existed in v1; its renaming as executable grounding is not a new component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methodology, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around the Logic Gap and executable grounding. BPRF and prompt terminology are renamed, methodology and experiments gain dedicated subsections, and definitions move into an appendix expanded into A.1–A.7. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The dataset-construction and framework diagrams are redrawn, performance tables gain color shading, and the dependency table changes from a wide horizontal display to a vertical model list. New radar and complexity plots are added. Dataset statistics and annotation illustrations move to the appendix, case tables are replaced, and the earlier DeepSeek output/reasoning figures are removed. The three dependency-example diagrams are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds a systematic comparison of eight existing benchmarks by size, modeling paradigm, and source (Appendix A.4, Table 6). It expands positioning against synthetic procedural datasets and schema-constrained instruction tuning, adding works including PET, ProcessTBench, and Pyrih et al. (2025). This goes beyond v1's narrative action-flow versus rule-flow distinction; the benchmark comparison is not an experimental baseline evaluation.

T1.justification: v3 explicitly normalizes complex conditions into atomic rules and specifies that equality operates on a single value (Appendices A.1 and A.7). This revises the semantics illustrated by grouped equality values in v1 Table 8 and Figure 11. The condition–action schema and dependency categories otherwise remain; added graph notation largely formalizes existing content, and no theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the limited empirical basis acknowledged in v1: broader regulatory coverage, matched Instruct/Thinking comparisons, systematic complexity tests, and concrete failure analyses make the findings more informative than aggregate scores and selected success cases alone. Clearer annotation guidance and reported code/data access also improve usefulness. Important weaknesses remain: error bars are undefined, and P5's small average leads in Tables 2–3 lack significance testing, limiting the stronger superiority claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ExIde business-rule extraction work. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, prompts, and appendices support comparison despite substantial benchmark and experimental revisions.

after.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of 13 LLMs in Tables 2–4, dependency-type and complexity analyses in Figures 3–4, annotation-quality measurements, and appendix case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 12 LLMs in Tables 4–6, annotation-quality measurements, and experimental case studies.

results.title: Business as Rulesual: A Benchmark and Framework for Business Rule Flow Modeling with LLMs

C1.justification: v2 adds a headline claim that ChainEval has the strongest correlation with expert judgments among tested metrics. Its abstract and conclusion emphasize finance- and math-tuned models substantially narrowing the frontier-model gap, revising v1's predominantly scale-driven account of general-purpose models outperforming specialized models. The central symbolic financial benchmark contribution remains.

C2.justification: v2 substantially revises explanations toward fine-tuning scope, domain accuracy versus generality, and structural alignment as a basis for metric validity. It adds specific limitations involving verbosity-inflated scores and repetitive outputs confusing regex parsing, with proposed parsing and length-penalty remedies. The earlier synthetic-data, numerical-task, and English/U.S. applicability limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the zero-shot prompt, regex step extraction, model identifiers and backbones (Table 3), expert qualifications, calibration and correction workflow, and human-rating rubrics (Appendices B–F). Project and leaderboard links supplement the retained code link. The template-generation prompt is retained, while the obsolete Claude verification prompt is removed. Newly disclosed prompting and parsing details alone do not establish changes to earlier runs.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from 54 to 58 topics by adding Stress Testing, Regulatory Compliance, Risk Appetite, and Risk Metrics within Risk Management (Figure 2). v2 also constrains questions to a single target value. The twelve domains and English, U.S.-based symbolic financial task remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated panel changes substantially from 30 to 26 models. v2 adds GPT-5 variants, Claude Sonnet models, Gemini 2.5, full DeepSeek models, Grok 4, and DianJin-R1, while removing Gemma variants, Mixtral, larger Llama models, o3/o4-mini, and FinanceConnect, among others. Its Finance-LlaMA and Finance-Qwen entries retain the WiroAI comparators under shorter names.

E3.justification: The primary scoring protocol changes to DTWNormGate, and ROUGE-Lsum disappears. v2 adds randomized, anonymized human assessment of 20 questions answered by five models and a separate 200-case comparison including Grok 4 Heavy. MetaMath's stated size changes from 13B to 7B, and fixed decoding settings gain an availability exception. Figure 4's ChainEval caption conflicts with its FAC axis, leaving that analysis's metric uncertain.

E4.justification: v2 adds human validation of ChainEval, gated-versus-soft and DTW-versus-non-DTW comparisons, template-error statistics, and analysis of verbosity and repetitive-step parsing failures (Section 5.2; Appendices D and G). The name-only, value-only, and combined perturbation experiment in v1 Section 5.3.4 and Table 2 is removed. Difficulty analysis remains with revised models and reporting.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly identifies Table 1 dispersions as standard deviations and introduces Spearman correlation estimation for human-rating and metric validation. Both versions retain ten random-seed instantiations per template; this does not establish additional repeated model runs. Neither provides confidence intervals or significance tests for the metric-ranking differences.

E6.justification: Benchmark results are extensively replaced under revised data and scoring. v2 Table 1 reports ChainEval scores of 58.65 for Gemini 2.5 Pro, 57.34 for Fin-R1, and 56.40 for Mathstral; these cannot be interpreted as gains over v1 FAC or Step-F1. New results include Grok 4 Heavy's 61.99 versus GPT-5's 60.60 on the shared 200-case subset and DTWNormGate's human correlation of 0.640. Earlier perturbation and comprehensive appendix domain results disappear.

M1.justification: Section 4 replaces independent maximum-similarity step matching and thresholded precision/recall/F1 with monotonic Dynamic Time Warping alignment and normalized gated path scoring. Section 3.3 also replaces Claude-triggered expert escalation with calibrated direct expert review and template corrections.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, construction narrative, and results discussion undergo extensive rewriting and compression. Model discussion is reorganized from six categories into four, metric validation precedes experimental setup, and the appendices are reorganized around expert auditing and metric evaluation. Author and affiliation text also changes.

P2.justification: Table 1 is redesigned with fewer metric columns, a model-size column, and different groupings. The main radar display changes from two panels to one, the difficulty plot is redrawn, and the comprehensive appendix radar figures are removed. New displays cover model sources, annotation errors, metric correlations, and annotation interfaces. Figure 4 introduces a caption/axis mismatch between ChainEval and FAC.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds comparisons with TAT-QA, MultiHiertt, DocMath-Eval, and FinanceMath. References also change with the evaluated model panel. This broadens the discussion of adjacent benchmarks while retaining the central positioning around explicit, executable, domain-aware financial reasoning supervision.

T1.justification: The formal metric definition changes from independently maximized, thresholded step alignment to normalized minimum-cost DTW path alignment. Appendix G adds a weighted soft similarity definition with weights 0.85 and 0.15. Equation 4 also changes the relative-error denominator to the absolute gold value, correcting its behavior for negative values. These are substantive mathematical changes, although neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps: v1 lacks human validation of ChainEval and relies on Claude-flagged expert checking, whereas v2 reports comprehensive expert review with 29 template corrections and validation against 100 human-rated responses. The metric ablations, explicit rubrics, and model identifiers substantially strengthen empirical grounding and auditability. Removing perturbation and detailed domain results, and introducing Figure 4's metric-label inconsistency, weaken parts of the evaluation but do not outweigh these central gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FinChain and ChainEval. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained content across the substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, a 200-case model comparison, expert template-audit outcomes, and human-rating correlations and metric ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 30 models on 2,700 generated cases, domain and difficulty analyses, and name/value perturbation experiments.

results.title: FinChain: A Symbolic Benchmark for Verifiable Chain-of-Thought Financial Reasoning

C1.justification: The introduction narrows its research-gap claim: v3 acknowledges temporally rich video diagnostics and complex reasoning benchmarks, emphasizing their lack of targeted user-feedback sycophancy evaluation. The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the benchmark and two mitigation contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning systematic versus decoding-noise errors, response-format dependence, preservation of ordinary accuracy and regression in newer commercial models. It also introduces an orthogonality interpretation for steering and explicit limitations concerning white-box access, hour-scale videos and agentic tasks. These substantially extend the scientific discussion.

D1.justification: The abstract changes the supplied code-access location from GitHub to an anonymous.4open.science repository. v3 documents three-path voting and manual response classification for new experiments. Existing hardware, separate 100-video calibration set, selected layers and PCA settings remain documented.

E1.justification: The MSVD, MSRVTT and NExT-QA coverage, 367 videos, 6,367 questions and seven sycophancy scenarios are retained. Added experiments reuse this video-QA coverage; relaxed response formatting changes the protocol rather than the underlying task.

E2.justification: v3 Section 5.3/Table 4 adds majority voting and contradiction-checking prompting as evaluated alternatives to both mitigation methods on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Appendix G also adds Gemini-2.5-Flash to the commercial-model comparison. Existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: v3 adds neutral-question accuracy evaluation over 6,367 questions and a relaxed-response protocol with manual classification of misleading and non-committal answers across five scenarios. The new majority-vote comparator uses three sampled decoding paths. These expand evaluation procedures without replacing the original benchmark protocol.

E4.justification: New Appendices A and D test whether mitigation harms ordinary answering accuracy and whether restricting responses to option letters drives observed sycophancy. These address important validation questions absent from v2. Existing frame-count, random-selection, architecture-failure, attention and steering-strength analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed-based replication, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. The CRS small-sample warning and attention displays are retained. Three sampled paths in the new voting baseline define that comparator, not an uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Existing numerical tables retain their values after matching relocations and transpositions. New results include average MSS of 44.71 for majority voting and 52.84 for contradiction prompting, neutral-accuracy losses of 1.13–3.74 percentage points, and relaxed-response misleading/non-committal rates of 36.00%/4.45%. Gemini-2.5-Flash adds average MSS/CRS of 64.39/20.09.

M1.justification: Both versions retain neutral-prompt key-frame selection and inference-time representation steering, including the appendix PCA-subspace intervention. v3 condenses explanations and adds an illustration without establishing a changed algorithm, calibration procedure or intervention.

P1.justification: Rewriting is concentrated in the introduction, Related Work and condensed key-frame explanation. v3 relocates limitations and calibration qualifications, removes the LLM-use declaration, and adds ethics and acknowledgements text. Most existing narrative and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 changes the document from one-column to two-column layout, transposes both main mitigation tables and relocates the complex-question table to Appendix B. It adds five result tables and a key-frame illustration. Existing benchmark, attention and case figures are retained, with resizing and relocation.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands citations concerning sycophancy, activation steering, multimodal trustworthiness and retrieval-based reasoning. The introduction and Related Work revise positioning to distinguish sycophancy from existing temporal-reasoning and factuality diagnostics. Missing steering citations are also resolved; bibliographic updates alone are excluded from this judgment.

T1.justification: The MSS/CRS notation is simplified to correct-to-incorrect and incorrect-to-correct counts without changing the definitions. Attention metrics, separability calculations and PCA intervention derivations are retained, with the steering appendix moving from F to H. No new proof or formal theoretical result appears.

improvement.justification: v2 lacked standard mitigation alternatives and quantified neutral-accuracy costs; v3 addresses these gaps in Tables 4 and 5. Table 8 additionally tests response-format dependence, substantially strengthening the empirical validation of both mitigation and benchmark design. The new checks cover limited model families, and accuracy preservation does not establish the claimed representation orthogonality, but the added controls provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VISE benchmark and mitigation methods. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds mitigation comparisons, neutral-question accuracy tests, relaxed-response experiments and Gemini-2.5-Flash evaluations.

before.justification: v2 reports original Video-LLM evaluations, mitigation experiments, attention analyses, ablations and qualitative cases in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Flattery in Motion: Benchmarking and Analyzing Sycophancy in Video-LLMs

C1.justification: v2 explicitly extends the claimed benefits to general-purpose VQA and scalability across six model sizes spanning three architectures. Its abstract, introduction, and conclusion foreground understanding vision-token information during hallucination. The earlier emphasis was efficient hallucination mitigation; the training-free decoding contribution and up-to-2x cost claim remain.

C2.justification: v2 refines the mechanism interpretation: visual input favors ground-truth objects overall, but the corresponding shift is not significant at hallucinated steps, where language priors can dominate. It also replaces the earlier threshold tradeoff discussion with a modest-sensitivity interpretation. Existing limitations concerning visually salient cues and unavailable external knowledge are retained in Appendix D.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly discloses top-p, top-k, and beam settings, diagnostic tokenization/alignment rules, HallusionBench judge inputs, and MMMU filtering and prompt instructions. Timing hardware information is revised, while AMBER resizing and DeepSeek repetition-penalty details disappear with those experiments. ReVisiT pseudocode, caching instructions, hyperparameter guidance, and code access remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 removes AMBER evaluation and adds HallusionBench's visual-dependent original/edited-image questions, MMMU multidisciplinary reasoning, and VQAv2 open-ended question answering. CHAIR, POPE's three datasets and query types, and LLaVA-Bench qualitative examples remain. Coverage expands substantially beyond the earlier hallucination-focused evaluation.

E2.justification: CODE is added as an evaluated comparator in the retained CHAIR, POPE, and latency comparisons, alongside the unchanged Greedy, DoLa, VCD, M3ID, and SID comparator set. It also participates in the new benchmark comparisons.

E3.justification: CHAIR reporting replaces Recall with mean per-caption F1. v2 adds five model configurations and removes the DeepSeekVL2 setting. New protocols include teacher-forced image-removal controls, GPT-4 judging on HallusionBench, and MMMU evaluation on 857 single-image items. The timing CPU changes from AMD EPYC 9354 to Intel Xeon Gold 5320. The retained CHAIR sample size/seed and POPE design remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic analyses of grounded alternatives at hallucinated steps, image-present versus image-absent predictions, and constrained versus full-vocabulary vision-token projections (Section 2). It adds random and maximum-JSD selection controls and expands the reported threshold sweep from three to six values (Table 10). Earlier qualitative cases and vocabulary/layer ablations are retained or extended.

E5.justification: Beyond v1's latency means and standard deviations, v2 introduces 95% Wilson intervals and paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Pratt handling and Holm-adjusted p-values for its diagnostic analyses (Appendix A.1). The existing CHAIR seed and latency practice of three decodes for each of 300 samples are retained.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive benchmark, diagnostic, scaling, and ablation results while removing AMBER and DeepSeekVL2 results. Retained scores also change: Qwen ReVisiT CHAIR_S/CHAIR_I become 29.8/7.04 instead of 31.6/7.56; POPE average accuracy changes from 84.77 to 84.53, now below SID's 85.78. These are revised reported results, not established method improvements. Latency values also change under a different reported CPU.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 retain adaptive vocabulary constraints, cached vision-token projections, minimum-JSD token/layer selection, and multiplicative output refinement. Notation and explanations change, but the proposed decoding procedure does not.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, motivation, experimental discussion, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Preliminary notation moves into Section 3; related work, the main qualitative discussion, and limitations move into appendices. The narrative shifts from prior-method motivation toward empirical investigation of vision tokens, beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 adds model-scaling and diagnostic plots, new benchmark/statistical tables, and an ablation plot with an expanded two-panel table. The retained overview becomes Figure 5, and the cartoon example moves from main-text Figure 4 to appendix Figure 9. The document template, headers, captions, table structures, and placement also change substantially.

R1.justification: The pre-/intra-/post-alignment taxonomy and detailed related-work discussion are retained in Appendix A.3. v2 adds vision-representation interpretation and retrieval-augmented-generation references, CODE, and new benchmark/model citations, while dropping several early-exit and removed-evaluation references. This refines positioning without replacing the established relationship to prior decoding approaches.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 introduces formal definitions for at-least-one recall@k, single-token ground-truth/hallucinated-object subsets, and paired probability contrasts. These formalize the new diagnostics; the core decoding mathematics remains equivalent, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly motivates its central design through illustrative examples and does not test minimum-JSD selection against random or maximum-JSD alternatives. v2 addresses these important evidence gaps through controlled vision-token analyses with statistical reporting and direct selection ablations (Section 2, Appendices A.1 and B.2). General VQA and model-scaling evaluations further strengthen applicability evidence. Although AMBER/MoE evidence is lost and some existing score revisions remain unexplained, the substantially stronger support for the method's rationale and scope outweighs these costs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReVisiT research work. All 23 pages of v1 and 30 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable, and retained methods, figures, tables, and qualitative examples can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, vision-token diagnostic analyses, model-scaling experiments, ablations, latency measurements, and qualitative results.

before.justification: v1 reports original CHAIR, POPE, AMBER, DeepSeekVL2, latency, ablation, and qualitative results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Revisit What You See: Revealing Visual Semantics in Vision Tokens to Guide LVLM Decoding

C1.justification: The abstract and four principal contributions remain substantially unchanged. The conclusion narrows the claim that tuned Llama outperforms all conventional LLMs to most conventional LLMs, while the introduction broadens its training discussion from Llama specifically to SLR-tuned models.

C2.justification: v5 adds a systematic-rule-induction explanation for transfer, model-specific explanations of abstraction failures and shortcut behavior, and interpretations of reasoning-trace degeneration. It also qualifies semantic leakage guarantees and cross-model compute comparisons, and discusses GRPO reward collapse beyond level 7. These substantially extend v3's interpretation of accuracy, syntax and compute trends.

D1.justification: v5 adds mirror-sampling details, error-detection heuristics, and brief Qwen3, GRPO and CLUTRR setup information. Table 5 adds GPT-5/Qwen3 pricing while dropping many earlier pricing entries. The explicit two-epoch, approximately 17k-example training description disappears, without establishing an actual budget change. Core hyperparameters, code/data links and licensing remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v5 adds SLR-Homes, comprising 500 house-classification tasks across five difficulty levels with different vocabulary and relational structure. It also evaluates CLUTRR kinship inference across six generalization and robustness variants. These substantially extend the represented evaluation domains beyond the retained train curriculum and downstream suite.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator set expands substantially through GPT-5 and Qwen3 families, including reasoning-enabled and disabled variants, plus CoT comparisons and DeepSeek-R1-8B on CLUTRR. Random and reverse curriculum controls are also added. Earlier leaderboard models remain represented in the extended Table 16 despite omissions from the shortened main table.

E3.justification: New protocols include curriculum-order comparisons on levels 5–7 with matched data and token budgets, shuffled Qwen3 fine-tuning, and GRPO training stopped at level 7. v5 also introduces greedy-decoding CLUTRR evaluation and multi-completion Pass@1/4/8 and CoT testing. These are added experimental designs; the PDFs do not establish why existing leaderboard scores were revised.

E4.justification: Appendices E–G add synthesis-parameter comparisons, curriculum-order controls, cross-domain transfer tests, sampling/CoT sensitivity, and quantified error, shortcut and output-length analyses. These address questions largely untested in v3. Conversely, the o4-mini comparison in Table 9 and the relocated compute plot reuse earlier evidence.

E5.justification: Appendix F.4 newly states that Pass@k scores for k below 8 are averaged and discusses variability across sampled completions. This adds limited sampling and aggregation information, without establishing repeated training runs. Neither version reports training seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests.

E6.justification: Existing reported values change: base/tuned Llama LRL moves from 3.6/8.8 to 3.8/8.7, and GPT-4.5 LRL from 7.6 to 7.3. New results include base/tuned Llama accuracy of 10.3%/42.3% on SLR-Homes and 25.5%/32.1% on CLUTRR, alongside Qwen3, GRPO and diagnostic results. Separate MMLU-CS/ML results disappear. Unexplained revisions to older scores do not establish same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the symbolic judge remain unchanged. Appendix F.3 adds a concrete GRPO training variant for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, extending the demonstrated training procedure beyond SFT. v3 already described generic RLVR support, so this is a limited training adaptation.

P1.justification: Although the main section sequence remains, v5 substantially reorganizes existing appendix material into notation, benchmark details and training sections. It condenses the main reward exposition, adds task notation and a motivating example, and restructures the findings narrative around transfer, curriculum order and error modes.

P2.justification: v5 adds extensive dedicated displays for ablations, training variants, sampling results and failure analyses, plus an expanded leaderboard with organization symbols and a reasoning-enabled column. It also restructures the downstream table, moves the curriculum table and compute plot into the appendices, and changes caption placement. The original framework diagrams are largely retained.

R1.justification: v5 adds positioning against classic ILP datasets through Mutagenesis, cites De Raedt's learning-from-entailment framework, and adds the DeepSeekMath reference for GRPO. References to Fourrier's leaderboard and Mondorf and Plank's benchmark are removed. The broader research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 refines the stated rule-length definition by excluding structural linking predicates, while Section 3 explicitly states the closed-world assumption. The existing FOL definitions and entailment-based reward equations are retained and relocated; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: SLR-Homes and CLUTRR directly strengthen evidence for transfer beyond the train domain, while Qwen3 and GRPO experiments broaden validation beyond v3's single Llama SFT demonstration. Quantified failure analyses also make the framework's boundaries more assessable. These are substantial evidential gains, despite weaknesses: some parameter comparisons are confounded, curriculum-order scores are nearly tied without uncertainty estimates, and explicit epoch information is lost.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SLR framework and SLR-BENCH. All 20 pages of v3 and 26 pages of v5, including appendices, are readable, and retained methods, equations, figures and tables can be matched across relocations.

after.justification: v5 retains original evaluations and adds transfer experiments, training comparisons, ablations and quantitative error analyses in Tables 7–16.

before.justification: v3 reports original LLM evaluations and Llama fine-tuning results on SLR-BENCH and downstream benchmarks in Tables 3–4.

results.title: SLR: Automated Synthesis for Scalable Logical Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the claims from country–relation tasks to factual and linguistic concept–relation prediction. They newly claim that components capture concepts more comprehensively than individual features while maintaining specificity. The original causal-intervention and composability claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of verb-steering failures, including unstable components, polysemanticity, and context-dependent relations. It interprets cross-task interference as evidence of differing specificity and expands limitations to manual component selection, combinatorial scaling, small datasets, model knowledge, and transcoder reconstruction errors.

D1.justification: Appendices B–C newly provide complete main-task concept and accepted-answer lists, handling of semantic and grammatical variants, and explicit extraction and evaluation prompts. Appendices G and L add linguistic-task steering strengths and transcoder tuning details. These substantially expand documentation beyond v1's limited country-task templates and hyperparameter information.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained ten-country factual tasks, v2 evaluates translation of eleven English words into Spanish, French, and German, and five transformations of eight verbs. Appendix K additionally reports a study of class, order, and family relationships for 26 animals.

E2.justification: v2 Section 3.4 adds one explicit comparator for country-fact steering: intervening on the single feature whose individual ablation produces the highest KL divergence. v1 lacks this steering comparison. Function vectors and other cited approaches are discussed but are not additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce a highest-KL single-feature control, accuracy evaluation across tasks with overlapping pairs excluded for same-task tests, and transcoder-specific settings including correlation threshold 0.7 and steering strength 13. The retained country-fact prompts and steering strengths are unchanged; newly documented answer lists do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 tests whether whole components outperform individual features and whether component ablations interfere with other tasks (Sections 3.4–3.5). It extends node-level organization analyses to linguistic tasks, adds taxonomic hierarchy and clustering analyses, and investigates transcoder transfer and resistance to feature ablation (Appendices J–L).

E5.justification: Both versions report point success rates and node-level KL-divergence plots with fitted regression lines. v2 adds no repeated-run or seed reporting, confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or changed uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: v2 Table 2 adds concept/relation/composite steering rates of .75/.92/.59 for translation and .48/.26/.22 for verbs, alongside new baseline, interference, taxonomy, and 27% transcoder results. Country-result reporting also changes: the composite average is .90 in v1 Table 6 and .92 in v2 Table 2, but v2 Table 20 retains .90 despite revised cells. These inconsistent reports do not establish a reliable country-steering gain.

M1.justification: The core feature-selection, correlation-graph, density-pruning, and connected-component pipeline remains. v2 adds task-specific adaptations: grouping multiple causal components for translation and verbs, using prompt-specific verb components, and a transcoder variant that omits density pruning and retains language-unique nodes (Section 3.1; Appendix L).

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively reframed around relational reasoning, related work moves after the experiments, and the numbered method pipeline becomes condensed descriptive paragraphs. The discussion becomes a conclusion plus expanded standalone limitations, and the appendices are substantially reorganized into thematic sections.

P2.justification: v2 switches to a two-column layout, consolidates component and layer plots into Figures 3–4, and introduces a cross-task steering summary and many new displays. Detailed country tables move to appendices, main examples are shortened and mixed across tasks, and steering tables gain answer highlighting. Retained word clouds and Gemma 2 9B figures are relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused references concerning function vectors, individual-feature steering, taxonomy, language networks, and neuronal population coding. It develops the connection to Merullo et al.'s relational vector arithmetic, while retaining the central positioning around SAE coactivation and efficient alternatives to exhaustive circuit tracing.

T1.justification: The core top-k feature-set and correlation-graph mathematics remain unchanged. Omitting the explicit standard Pearson-correlation formula is an explanatory edit. v2 introduces no new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v1 did not directly test the steering advantage of whole components over individual features or quantify interference with other tasks. v2 addresses both in Sections 3.4–3.5, while broader tasks expose meaningful failure conditions and fuller prompts and answer criteria improve auditability. These substantially strengthen the paper's empirical justification and applicability boundaries. The gains outweigh localized reporting weaknesses, particularly the inconsistent country composite totals in Tables 2 and 20.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SAE feature-coactivation research despite retitling and expanded scope. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching and comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original country-fact experiments and reports additional translation, verb-transformation, single-feature comparison, cross-task, taxonomy, and transcoder results.

before.justification: v1 reports original component-ablation, steering, and layer-organization experiments on Gemma 2 2B, with Gemma 2 9B results in Appendix C.

results.title: Sparse Feature Coactivation Reveals Causal Semantic Modules in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central claims about supervised calibration, demographic variation, and the benchmark remain. v2 withdraws practical survey-prediction guidance as an explicit contribution and emphasizes distributional alignment and consistency. Its introduction also revises the minimal-supervision claim from five examples to one to ten.

C2.justification: v2 adds an 'overthinking' hypothesis for Claude's CoT failures and connects incomplete distribution extraction with higher variability. Its discussion explicitly limits the intended application by saying the method should not replace human survey respondents. Most interpretations concerning demographic disparities, calibration, and post-training are retained.

D1.justification: v2 specifies scikit-learn, explicitly identifies 270 dataset-LLM-elicitation-prompt regressors, details training-example construction and the supervision-size schedule, and identifies the OLMo checkpoints as used out of the box through Hugging Face. Appendix B adds CoT and few-shot templates, while Appendix C documents extraction completeness. These primarily extend documentation; both versions retain the same future code/data-release promise.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 92 questions from WGM, OpinionQA, and WVS and retain the same demographic coverage and held-out-dataset scenarios. v2's expanded demographic overview consolidates groups already represented in v1's results.

E2.justification: v2 adds CoT prompting as a comparator for Claude-3.5-v2 and OLMo-2-7B-Instruct in Table 2, and five-shot prompting for the five main LLMs in Table 4. These substantially extend the alternatives evaluated against calibration beyond v1's standard base and SD prompting and retained elicitation comparisons.

E3.justification: Section 3.6 changes the stated train/development/test split from 60/20/20 to 80/10/10, resolving the conflict with v1 Section 6's statement of 80% training. New comparisons match the five examples supplied to prompting and calibration and impose a 500-word CoT response limit. Unchanged retained scores do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a qualitative CoT failure case involving exaggerated demographic differences and an extraction-failure audit in Appendix C, with discussion of refusals and formatting failures. Existing demographic, supervision-size, post-training, and out-of-domain analyses remain; moving the generalization discussion and MSE plots does not add analyses.

E5.justification: The new three-way comparisons report ANOVA followed by paired t-tests and Bonferroni correction. Five-shot results average three random example selections, while the existing supervision-size study retains ten samples. v2 also makes the significance-testing procedure more explicit for retained comparisons.

E6.justification: Matched existing alignment tables retain their numerical values, but Tables 2, 4, and 17 add substantial results. For example, v2 reports WGM base-verbalized OLMo alignment of 86.1 with CoT alongside 59.8 with standard prompting and 85.1 with calibration. Few-shot results reveal additional exceptions to calibration's advantage, and extraction rates document missing outputs. The convergence summary changes from around five examples to one to ten on retained curves.

M1.justification: The proposed method still fits answer-probability regressions using human distributions, selects among linear, lasso, ridge, and random-forest regressors, and renormalizes predictions. Section 3.6 expands its explanation; CoT and few-shot prompting are evaluated alternatives, not new calibration components.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the title, abstract, introduction, and related-work narrative; expands calibration into structured explanatory subsections; removes the standalone practitioner-guidance section; and condenses the post-training discussion. Generalization moves to the appendix, while the supervision-size figure moves into the main text. This is substantial rewriting and reorganization beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds comparison Tables 2 and 4, prompt-variation Table 16, and extraction Table 17; substantially restructures the demographic overview; and adds performance highlighting to Table 1. The unchanged MSE panels move from appendix Figure 4 into main-text Figure 3 and are vertically rearranged. Most existing appendix result tables retain their displays apart from numbering and positioning.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands from SD prompting and confidence elicitation into social alignment, probabilistic reasoning, and distributional alignment. New discussions include Meister et al., Cao et al., and Hashemi et al., positioning supervised calibration relative to distribution elicitation, divergence-loss fine-tuning, and other alignment approaches.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.4 introduces a written metric definition averaging (1-WD)/(N-1), whereas v1 describes 1-Wasserstein distance. Dividing the entire numerator is not an equivalent rewrite, and N is not defined beyond identifying N-1 as a normalization factor. This creates a limited mathematical specification ambiguity; it does not establish changed computation. The calibration mathematics otherwise remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 left CoT and in-context learning untested. v2's comparison using identical five-example supervision directly addresses whether regression adds value beyond supplying examples in the prompt, while CoT results clarify model-dependent alternatives. Appendix C also exposes previously unexplained extraction failures. These substantially strengthen the central empirical case and its transparency. The ambiguous new normalization equation is a limited drawback, outweighed by the stronger controls and clearer documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same supervised distribution-calibration study despite the changed title. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds chain-of-thought and few-shot comparisons and distribution-extraction statistics.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM experiments on three survey datasets, including calibration, demographic comparisons, supervision-size experiments, post-training analyses, and cross-dataset generalization.

results.title: Improving the Distributional Alignment of LLMs using Supervision

C1.justification: The headline claims expand from debugging and constrained-kernel optimization to demonstrated natural-language generation gains and neural-accelerator optimization. v3 claims a 41.8% relative generation improvement over Gemini-3-pro and replaces v2's 82.7% repair and 3.6× DSL/learning comparison headlines with 32.6% relative debugging improvement and 3.3× over RALAD. The overall ChatHLS purpose remains.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of retrieval's differing effects on generation and debugging, model-scaling behavior, optimization trajectories and physical feasibility. Appendix G acknowledges greater hardware costs and lower resource efficiency than methods such as Allo. New limitations explicitly identify unsupported DATAFLOW/AXI directives and validation on only one FPGA platform, substantially qualifying v2's generalization discussion.

D1.justification: Appendices A–D newly disclose retrieval chunking, embedding/vector-store choices, top-k retrieval, log parsing, full prompts, teacher inputs, sampling temperatures, detailed SFT/DPO settings, software environment and training durations. These greatly extend v2's brief training description. Appendix H adds asset licensing and intended-use information without establishing a new public artifact release.

E1.justification: v3 adds 108 natural-language-to-HLS generation tasks, comprising 85 HLS-Eval designs and 23 custom designs. Optimization expands beyond v2's five linear-algebra kernels to broader kernel workloads and MobileNet and Transformer accelerators. Kernel/Vitis/Manual debugging coverage is retained; changed case counts alone do not establish new coverage.

E2.justification: Debugging comparators change from GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama3.1-8B and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B to Gemini-3-pro, Claude-opus-4.5, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and DeepSeek-V3.2. v3 also adds matched RAG variants and C2HLSC/HLSRewriter comparisons; Appendix D.3 identifies the latter baselines as published scores. RALAD and the DSL/learning-based optimization comparators remain.

E3.justification: Training changes from Llama3-8B with 11 SFT/3 DPO epochs to Qwen2.5-Coder-14B with 3/2 epochs; training sample counts and the debugging test size also change. v3 introduces staged pass@k evaluation, matched retrieval controls, an explicit 80% resource ceiling and post-route checks. Optimization is reported as 15 trials, although five-iteration descriptions remain, leaving the exact budget relationship unresolved.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained HLSFixer component ablation, v3 adds train–test similarity analysis, controlled retrieval studies, model-family/size sensitivity, token-cost analyses and optimization trajectories in Appendices D–G. Table 4 adds physical-feasibility validation after place-and-route. The per-error analysis expands from 24 displayed error types to 33.

E5.justification: v2 reports aggregate pass rates without repeated-sampling counts or uncertainty bars. v3 specifies five candidates per debugging case and 20 generation repetitions, uses sampled pass@k estimation, and adds error bars to Figure 6 and token-cost Figures 15 and 17. These are newly reported practices; seeds and the statistical meaning of the bars remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Reported debugging performance changes from 82.7% on 612 cases to 93.4% pass@1 on 591 cases. Figure 9's optimization headline changes from 5.4× over baseline on five kernels to 18.1× over broader workloads. These use changed models and evaluation conditions, so they are not same-setting gains. v3 adds generation, accelerator, retrieval and physical-implementation results and removes the energy-efficiency proxy results.

M1.justification: v3 extends generation inputs from C algorithms to include natural-language descriptions and changes SFT from LoRA adaptation to full-parameter tuning. The VODA workflow, hierarchical diagnosis/fixing/judging, DPO and three-directive optimization loop remain. The expanded reasoning-to-instruction and QoR-aware reasoning descriptions largely elaborate existing mechanisms.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around three challenges, and contributions are reordered. Method exposition changes from workflow–VODA–HLSFixer–HLSTuner to workflow–HLSTuner–HLSFixer–VODA. Numbered sections, expanded explanations, structured appendices and dedicated limitations/ethics sections substantially reorganize the narrative; author and affiliation text also changes.

P2.justification: v3 redraws introductory visuals, expands the optimization chart, and adds generation/accelerator/RAG tables plus prompt, similarity, scaling, cost and trajectory figures. v2's Table 2 is retained as v3's Table 6, and its per-error Figure 6 is expanded and relocated as Figure 14. The energy-efficiency chart is removed, alongside extensive plot and page-layout changes.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 expands positioning beyond retrieval-based assistance to recent LLM-based Bayesian directive optimization and GNN-supervised LIFT, emphasizing design–directive–QoR relationships. References add HLS-Eval, C2HLSC, HLSDebugger and other recent work while removing several earlier general code/HDL and retrieval references. This revises the competitive context beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2's bespoke nonlinear Energy Efficiency definition and its latency/resource penalty construction in Equation 2 are removed. v3 instead formalizes resource-constrained speedup in Appendix D.4. Neither version contains substantive theorems or proofs; the additional standard metric formulas do not constitute a major theoretical contribution.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps in v2's narrow optimization validation and limited implementation disclosure through broader workloads, matched RAG controls, detailed training/prompt settings and post-place-and-route validation. Explicit applicability limits and resource-cost discussion also improve the paper's qualification of its claims. These provide substantial gains in evidential support and reproducibility, despite unresolved five-versus-fifteen optimization budgets and undefined error bars; higher headline scores alone do not establish the improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ChatHLS research, with identifiable retained methods and experiments. All text, equations, tables and figures were readable, including v3's Appendices A–H. The supplied v2 ends with references and contains no appendix.

after.justification: v3 reports original generation, debugging and optimization results, alongside retrieval controls, model-scaling analyses and post-implementation hardware measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original debugging experiments on 612 cases, HLSFixer ablations, and optimization experiments on five PolyBench kernels.

results.title: ChatHLS: Towards Systematic Design Automation and Optimization for High-Level Synthesis

C1.justification: The central chaos-informed discriminator and Lattice/ConformerNeXt contributions remain. V2 narrows the abstract's four-new/seven-total discriminator account to the two proposed chaos-informed critics, aligning it with the existing method. It drops v1's faster-inference promise and shifts application emphasis toward TTS and ASR; the 40x discriminator-size and approximately half-parameter claims already appeared in v1's body.

C2.justification: Appendix A.1 expands the mechanism explanation through vocal-fold/vocal-tract coupling and intermittent chaos. V2 removes explicit limitations concerning low-resource generalization and extra training/inference time while retaining the single-dataset, noise-free restriction. Appendix A.9 nevertheless newly interprets listening results as noisy/reverberant robustness without documenting such testing, and its 2% preference advantage conflicts with Figure 4's 11-point margin.

These substantially expand reproducibility information, although Table 9's one-GPU setting conflicts with Section 3.2's four GPUs, and some discriminator specifications remain inconsistent.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate English VCTK speech across the same nine bandwidth-extension ranges. V2's listening study uses ranges already covered in v1. TTS/ASR applications and noisy/reverberant robustness are discussed without documenting additional evaluated tasks or environments.

AP-BWE remains, while MS-BWE and its two reported LSD entries are removed. NU-Wave's empty row also disappears, but v1 provides no results establishing its evaluated participation.

The stated 50-epoch budget, batch size, optimizer settings and six objective metrics remain unchanged. Newly disclosed splits, segmentation and listening procedures do not establish changes to previously used procedures.

E4.justification: The discriminator, generator and frequency-range analyses are largely retained, with one revised generator-ablation result. V2 adds a male/female MOS breakdown and a concrete reconstruction example replacing dummy spectrograms. The subgroup definition is inconsistent: Section 3.11 refers to speakers, whereas Appendix A.9 refers to participants.

E5.justification: Appendix A.3 and Table 9 newly disclose seed 1234. Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. V2's claims of significant listener preference are not accompanied by a statistical testing procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds complete EBEN/AERO scores and listening outcomes: Figure 4 reports overall MOS 4.42 versus AP-BWE's 4.36 and preferences of 52% versus 41%. M1.justification: The dual-stream Lattice/ConformerNeXt generator and final four-discriminator combination are retained. V2 newly specifies losses and per-scale SRDs without establishing whether these changed the procedure or document existing implementation. Its MRLD description also says 2D convolution while Figure 2 and Table 7 specify 1D, preventing a reliable judgment about an actual architectural change.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the abstract, introduction and conclusion, merges introduction and related work, renames the model throughout and replaces the original repetitive opening with a structured motivation and contribution list. It also adds dedicated loss and subjective-analysis sections, acknowledgments and a nine-part appendix.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the mismatched architecture drawing and duplicated dummy spectrograms with a relevant architecture diagram, discriminator schematic and reconstruction example. It adds MOS/preference plots, the listening interface, a loss table and three implementation tables. The baseline table also changes metric order and row formatting, beyond its numerical updates.

R1.justification: The integrated introduction and related work substantially expand coverage of modern BWE, phase modeling, discriminator families, TTS/ASR applications and physiological chaos. Appendix A.1 adds extensive research context for speech dynamics. New references include Peng et al., Kong et al., Herzel et al., Feng et al. and Haws and Cui; v2 also explicitly acknowledges its substantial adaptation of AP-BWE code.

T1.justification: V2 Section 2.3 and Table 1 add explicit mathematical definitions of the weighted generator losses and summed discriminator hinge objective, including Equations 4–5. The Lyapunov estimator, reconstruction equations and convolution-complexity reasoning are retained. No theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: V1 lacks an explicit training objective, contains a mismatched architecture figure and leaves most baseline comparisons unreported. V2 substantially resolves these deficiencies through loss definitions, relevant diagrams, detailed implementation documentation, completed EBEN/AERO comparisons and actual listening outcomes. Removing MS-BWE and introducing conflicting hardware, discriminator and subjective-result descriptions limit confidence; unsupported robustness language also weakens interpretation.
