Unlearning moves into the alternative-techniques discussion, applications move to Appendix D, and discussion/limitations topics are reorganized. The appendices expand from A–C to A–I with additional explanatory sections and analyses.

P2.justification: v2 adds full-width merging and eight-feature matrices in Tables 8–9 and separate PWD + CB and 70B comparisons in Tables 12–13. Table 1 gains a comparator row, Algorithm 1 gains a separate routine block, and several tables move. Original appendix Tables 8–9 become Tables 10–11. Both original figures retain identical graphics, with caption edits.

R1.justification: Sections 2–3 add pay-to-unlock literature and substantially revise the assessment of prior defenses. Table 1 changes existing methods' utility-preservation ratings from satisfied to unsatisfied and naive-jailbreak resistance from unsatisfied to satisfied, while recognizing Hofstätter et al.'s circuit-breaking robustness. Additional citations cover circuit breakers, preference/adversarial training, PEFT and vLLM.

T1.justification: The FLoTE mapping, loss expressions, perturbation optimization and spectral-norm formulas retain their mathematical substance. Naming the averaged refusal loss Lrobust and adding an informal feature definition clarify existing concepts; no new theorem, proof or substantive formal assumption appears.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly left broader model coverage and scalability beyond four features unresolved. v2 substantially strengthens these central aspects through 70B and eight-feature evaluations, a stronger PWD + CB comparator, expanded merging comparisons, and runtime and stochastic-decoding checks. Updated table entries also improve consistency. The new experiments usefully expose locking and utility limitations, although the abstract's perfect-locking and 7% headline claims need clearer scope in light of those results, and uncertainty reporting remains limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Locket research work. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds larger-model, eight-feature, additional-comparator, runtime and stochastic-inference results in Section 7 and Appendices F–I.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 and Appendix C report original measurements of feature locking, utility, jailbreak resistance and scalability across three language models.

results.title: Locket: Robust Feature-Locking Technique for Language Models

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes reward enrichment and fuller candidate utilization. V2 centers its contribution on recovering intermediate partial-error signals through semantic gating and hierarchical contrasts. The headline empirical claim changes from 7B competitiveness on WMT21–22 to effectiveness across 4B/9B models and 9B parity with GPT-4o/Gemini on the revised benchmarks.

C2.justification: V2 develops explanations involving sparse errors in the 'Zone of Uncertainty,' model confidence as a stabilizer, and SAC's complementarity with continuous QE. It adds interpretations of weighting tradeoffs and proprietary independence. A new limitations section explicitly addresses larger-model scalability, low-resource languages, and commercial-API reproducibility.

D1.justification: V2 adds the SAC prompt, exact proprietary-model versions, sequence length, warmup and clipping settings, vLLM use, H100 hardware and training time, API cost accounting, dataset statistics, and filtering details. It also supplies a code-availability link. V1 provides substantially less implementation and resource documentation.

E1.justification: V2 adds WMT23/WMT24 evaluation and IWSLT spoken-domain training; WMT21 disappears and WMT22 becomes training material. Language coverage changes from English↔{Czech, German, Icelandic, Chinese, Russian} to English↔{Chinese, German, Japanese}. FLORES-200 and HalOmi remain in use.

E2.justification: New evaluated comparators include Set-MPO, LiPO, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Aya models, TowerInstruct, and GRPO/GSPO. NLLB is removed. Standard DPO leaves the main benchmark comparison but remains alongside KTO, SimPO, ORPO, and CPO in objective-generalization experiments.

FLORES-test moves from training to held-out evaluation. V2 adds stratified blind human evaluation and matched-reward online-RL controls.

E4.justification: V2 adds model-confidence and partial-error distribution analyses, SAC and alternative-reward ablations, proprietary-dependence controls, data scaling, gold-reference SFT comparisons, and ranking/curriculum sensitivity studies. Existing component ablations are revised. V1's three-way comparison of many-versus-many, many-versus-one, and one-versus-many pairing is removed.

E5.justification: V1 Figure 1 explicitly displays mean XCOMET with a one-standard-deviation band; v2 Figure 2 uses box-and-whisker distributions, without specifying the whisker convention. This changes dispersion reporting. Neither version provides training-run counts, seeds, benchmark confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V1's WMT21–22 ALMA results are replaced by results under different benchmarks and backbones, including v2's WMT23 Gemma-M2PO averages of 97.87 Coverage and 89.67 XCOMET. Human evaluations and numerous control results are added. The retained HalOmi XCOMET hallucination correlation also changes from 0.7061 to 0.6972 after rescaling v2 Table 8; this is not rounding.

M1.justification: V1's additive KIWI-XXL plus WSPAlign reward becomes multiplicative gating by an LLM-based Semantic Alignment Classifier (SAC). V2 also revises confidence fusion, replaces softmax-weighted preference learning plus single-best behavior cloning with margin-weighted pairwise CPO, and changes the ranking target from static to fused scores (Section 4).

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work, motivation, and method narrative, organizing the method around two conceptual components. The appendix structure expands from A–B to A–J, with existing metric analysis and prompts relocated and expanded. The title, author list, and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the framework, replaces the original metric line plot with three boxplot panels, and moves the updated quality–faithfulness scatterplot to the first page. It restructures main tables around Coverage/XCOMET pairs and colored model groups, separates the pairing illustration, and adds distribution, scaling, case-study, sensitivity, and implementation displays.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially expanded and repositioned around online versus offline alignment and reward reliability versus data efficiency. V2 introduces discussion of Set-MPO, LiPO, GRPO, and GSPO, and explicitly argues that set/listwise methods inherit unreliable MT rewards. Traditional word alignment is newly contrasted with SAC as inadequate for subtle semantic errors.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions change substantially: additive reward becomes discrete multiplicative gating, confidence becomes length-normalized with sigmoid fusion, pair weights become normalized margins, and the listwise target changes (v1 Equations 2–9; v2 Equations 2–7). These revise the formal objective, although neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation through direct human assessment, additional controlled comparisons, matched-reward online-RL experiments, and an open-source pipeline test that better separates optimization gains from proprietary supervision. Expanded implementation details and explicit limitations improve transparency. Narrower language coverage, continued absence of run-level uncertainty, and an unexplained static-only ablation discrepancy between Tables 5 and 16 limit the conclusions, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe successive versions of M2PO for machine translation. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive revision.

after.justification: V2 reports original WMT23, WMT24, and FLORES-200 experiments, a 450-instance human evaluation, and extensive analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original WMT21–22 translation experiments, HalOmi metric analyses, preference-method comparisons, and ablations, including appendix results.

results.title: M^2PO: Multi-Perspective Multi-Pair Preference Optimization for Machine Translation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the central claims: directly optimizing KG construction through RL, introducing two task-aware rewards, and improving downstream QA utility. The additional comparisons strengthen the supporting evidence rather than redefine the principal contributions.

C2.justification: New Section 7 discusses dependence on frozen retrievers, reward-computation overhead, untested large-model and multilingual generalization, and the need for associated supporting passages. Appendix A adds substantive interpretations of RL versus RAFT, judge capacity, transferability, and reward-dependent graph structure.

D1.justification: Section 5.6 newly reports training times for four configurations and a 2–5-document pool for graph-retrieval training. E2.justification: v3 Tables 5–6 add evaluated zero-shot constructors DeepSeek-V3, GPT-5-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, Qwen3-235B, and gemini-2.5-flash-lite, plus reward-ranked fine-tuning through RAFT. Appendix A adds offline reward-filtering and fine-tuning, a 3B-versus-7B reward-judge comparison, testing within the official HippoRAG implementation, and structural count/diversity measurements. These substantially extend the evaluation design without establishing changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses testing whether on-policy RL outperforms reward-guided offline training, sensitivity to judge capacity, transfer to an existing HippoRAG pipeline, and how rewards affect graph topology. The F1-reward ablation, training curves, and two qualitative case studies already existed in v1 and are largely relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and training curves without experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional descriptive graph statistics do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial numerical evidence in Tables 4–8 and 12. For example, RAFT achieves 41.77 average ToG F1 versus GRPO's 41.28, while the separate official-HippoRAG experiment reports 32.09 versus 32.47 average F1. Original benchmark scores are retained; two Qwen-3B PopQA recall-gain annotations are corrected from 4.20 to 3.50 and 3.40 to 3.20.

M1.justification: The constructor, frozen retrieval pipeline, two utility rewards, and GRPO optimization without KL regularization remain unchanged. The Llama repetition penalty moves to Appendix D. RAFT and different judge sizes are comparison experiments, not replacements for the proposed method.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: Llama results and adaptation move to appendices, the existing reward ablation moves into Section 5.5, and training-input construction moves into Section 4.3. Appendices are restructured, a limitations section is added, and the reproducibility section is removed, although much core prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 switches to two-column layout, revises Figure 1, consolidates the main F1/recall and reward-ablation tables, and separates Llama results into appendix tables. It adds several comparison, timing, and structural-statistics tables. Existing training plots and case-study displays are rearranged rather than newly generated evidence.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including RAFT, LightRAG, TERAG, AtlasKV, and prior RL-based KG reasoning, while removing the Llama 3 and HybridFlow references. Section 2.2 more explicitly distinguishes graph generation from corpora from refinement of existing KGs. The broader research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The graph definitions, reward equations, and clipped GRPO objective remain substantively unchanged. However, Section 4.3 removes v1's explicit mathematical definition of the policy probability ratio and associated token-sequence definitions, leaving a limited loss of formal specification. No new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: The larger-constructor comparisons and RAFT control substantially address v1's limited evidence against alternative constructors and training strategies. Judge-size, pipeline-transfer, and structural analyses, together with explicit limitations, make the central argument and its boundaries more assessable. Removed resource links and mathematical detail weaken documentation, and some new prose overstates uniform improvements, particularly around Table 8. Nevertheless, the added scientific comparisons provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoGraph-R1 and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Relocated and reformatted material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds constructor comparisons, RAFT and judge-size experiments, pipeline integration results, and graph-structure measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original QA performance, passage recall, intrinsic graph-quality evaluations, reward ablations, and training dynamics.

results.title: AutoGraph-R1: End-to-End Reinforcement Learning for Knowledge Graph Construction

C1.justification: V2 elevates downstream single-stage autoregressive TTS to a main contribution in the abstract, introduction and conclusion, claiming superior intelligibility and objective naturalness against leading pure autoregressive systems. V1's central claims concern codec reconstruction, semantic representations and disentanglement.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations linking reduced TTS speaker similarity to low token rate and training-data generalization differences to speaker diversity. It discusses UTMOS limitations using human-rating differences and recommends omitting semantic supervision under resource constraints. These substantive explanations and applicability qualifications are absent from v1.

D1.justification: V2 adds the Qwen3-0.6B checkpoint link, TTS vocabulary and prompt-construction details, and inference hardware and total parameter counts. Existing codec hyperparameters and code/model-access statements remain, but the precise HuBERT and speaker-verification access links in v1's Section 4.2 are removed.

Separately, v2 removes Mimi's 687.5-bps configuration from Table 2 while retaining Mimi in Table 1. The new TTS comparators substantially expand the comparison scope.

These are new experimental protocols; the original codec training setup is retained.

E4.justification: Appendix F adds a comparison of LibriSpeech-only and mixed-corpus training, including training-versus-test speaker-similarity analysis. Appendix H tests how removing auxiliary losses affects ARCH representations, extending the existing reconstruction ablations. Appendix G additionally analyzes inference efficiency.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new listening study and other v2 experiments report point estimates without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 9–13 add substantial results, including English TTS WER of 1.06%, Chinese CER of 0.90%, reconstruction MOS of 3.94 versus 3.98 for ground truth, and SAC RTF of 0.0135. Tables 1 and 3–8 and the retained rows of Table 2 are unchanged; Mimi's low-bitrate result row is removed.

M1.justification: The SAC codec architecture and losses remain unchanged, but Section 5.4 and Appendix D add a substantive downstream generation procedure: a Qwen3-0.6B TTS model with an expanded dual-codebook vocabulary, fixed 1:2 semantic/acoustic token interleaving, and text- and audio-prompt-conditioned autoregressive inference.

P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract, contribution list and conclusion, adds Section 5.4 and appendix subsections, and makes localized terminology edits. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact; the original spectrogram Appendix D becomes Appendix I.

P2.justification: New Tables 9–13 substantially expand the presentation with TTS, listening-study, data-scale, speed and semantic-ablation displays. Table 2 loses the Mimi row, Table 4 moves, and Figure 4 relocates with the spectrogram appendix. The original figures are retained rather than replaced.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Seed-TTS, Qwen3, Llama and Libri-light, and positions its single-stage TTS procedure against VALL-E's two-stage pipeline and other autoregressive systems. The existing codec-related-work discussion and positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1–4 are retained, with no new proofs, assumptions or formal results. The added standard RTF definition supports an empirical metric rather than new theoretical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of SAC's intended use: v1 proposed speech-language-model applications without directly testing downstream generation, whereas v2 adds zero-shot TTS evidence. Human ratings independently support perceptual-quality claims, and data-scale and auxiliary-loss analyses clarify practical behavior. TTS attribution remains limited by different backbones and training corpora, MOS lacks uncertainty estimates, and removing a baseline and evaluation links creates small losses. Nevertheless, the added validation materially improves the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SAC research work. All pages, including equations, tables, figures and appendices, are readable, and retained experiments and relocated material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds TTS experiments, human listening scores, training-data-scale comparisons, speed measurements and semantic-representation ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original SAC reconstruction, representation, ablation and disentanglement results, including noisy-speech experiments in Appendix C.

results.title: SAC: Neural Speech Codec with Semantic-Acoustic Dual-Stream Quantization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and summary retain the same contributions and claims about speculative indexing-time context, future-context leakage, and approximately 9–11 percentage-point accuracy gains.

Section 4.1 adds cache-refresh and cost-amortization considerations. The original limitations and risk discussions are retained.

These are agent judgments; calibration, confidence intervals, and repeated-run uncertainty for benchmark scores remain unreported.

P1.justification: The original main narrative and retained appendix prose are largely unchanged. V2 adds an appendix contents page, dedicated sections, updated cross-references, and localized method and deployment explanations while preserving the existing narrative order.

P2.justification: V2 changes the appendix from full-width single-column pages to a continuous two-column layout, reflowing code listings and tables. It adds Algorithm 1 and Figures 4–5, redraws Figure 2 while retaining its example, and rearranges the Appendix A tables.

R1.justification: The related-work text and bibliography are unchanged after accounting for reflow. The positioning relative to code models, repository retrieval, and indexing-time computation remains the same.

T1.justification: Algorithm 1 introduces notation for the already-described context composition and caching procedure. No substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations are added or revised.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important reproducibility gap by supplying previously missing agent prompts, execution details, and experimental parameters in Appendices B and H. Appendix G also makes the explanatory arguments more inspectable. Its earlier, privileged oracle limits direct conclusions about SpecAgent, but the documentation gains substantially improve the paper despite unchanged headline accuracy results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SpecAgent study. Their text, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial appendix expansion and reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds LLM-judged analyses of retrieval successes and failures in Appendix G.

before.justification: V1 reports original REPOCOD-based code-completion experiments, including pass@1, latency, component ablations, and experiments with different agent backbones.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central claims of stable iterative global pruning, nested subnetworks enabling once-for-all deployment, and task-aligned importance improving downstream performance. The expanded model evidence in the abstract supports these retained contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of calibration robustness and subsequent adaptation, conjectures explaining SparseLLM's limited gains under structured pruning, and architecture-specific explanations contrasting Llama2 and Qwen3 sparsity patterns. The original limitations concerning computational cost and untested MoE architectures remain.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important validation and documentation gaps through calibration-budget and seed studies, explicit implementation specifications, and measured inference costs. results.title: From Local to Global: Revisiting Structured Pruning Paradigms for Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion replace v1's explicit causal framing with systematic-association language and add the conclusion that controlled experiments distinguish reasoning from generic RL and instruction-following degradation. This materially qualifies the central explanatory claim, although the introduction still claims reasoning-focused RL inherently amplifies hallucination. The benchmark contribution and reliability–capability trade-off remain.

C2.justification: v2 increasingly interprets representation changes as drift accompanying hallucination rather than an established causal mechanism. It adds interpretations distinguishing hallucination from general instruction-following failure and discussing drift even on the tool-training domain. New limitations explicitly acknowledge incomplete mechanistic causality and restricted mitigation coverage.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly documents screening 349 candidate tools into 296×2 pairs, distinct query formulations, and review by two annotators with third-reviewer adjudication. ReCall execution and CKA extraction details are expanded, and the abstract adds a code/data repository link. These primarily improve disclosure without establishing that the retained benchmark or experiments changed.

E1.justification: Section 4.4.2 adds IFEval for basic instruction compliance, ComplexBench for multiple instruction constraints, and the BFCL Multi-Turn base subset for held-out tool-calling scenarios. These substantially broaden evaluation beyond the retained SynTool, GSM8K, and SimpleToolHalluBench coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds direct tool-use RL as a comparator in Table 2 and a Llama3.1-8B Instruct/R1-Distill pair in Table 1. Appendix B adds Qwen3-4B/235B, DeepSeek-V3/R1, and Kimi-K2 Instruct/Thinking comparisons. The earlier model pairs and mitigation comparators remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.4 introduces a matched training comparison that varies explicit reasoning while holding data, reward, optimizer, and hyperparameters constant, alongside independent instruction-following and tool-competence tests. Model configurations expand substantially. Section 5.2 also changes the reported discrimination metric from classification accuracy to accuracy minus 0.5; this does not establish that existing probes were rerun.

E4.justification: New Section 4.4 tests whether hallucination amplification reflects explicit reasoning, generic RL, or broader instruction-following degradation. Appendix E adds module-level and cross-domain CKA analyses for ReCall, extending the earlier representation study. The original qualitative example tables are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the experiments. Tables and plots retain point-estimate reporting. The added annotation-review details concern benchmark quality control rather than statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results: Table 2 reports NTA hallucination of 41.4% for direct tool-use RL versus 90.2% for think-then-act RL; Table 3 reports BFCL scores of 13.6 before and 23.5 after ReCall. Additional model and CKA results appear in the appendices. Earlier model-pair and mitigation values remain, while Section 5.2 revises attention/MLP summary scores from 0.06/0.07 to 0.02/0.04 under the revised metric definition.

M1.justification: The primary ReCall/GRPO training procedures, benchmark diagnostic, and prompting/DPO mitigation approaches are retained. Direct tool-use RL is introduced as an experimental control. Expanded implementation descriptions and revised probe scoring do not establish a change to the primary algorithm or architecture.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, mechanistic discussion, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting or condensation. v2 introduces separate Limitations and Ethical Considerations sections, reorganizes and expands the appendices, and updates authors and affiliations.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column preprint layout to two columns. Figure 1 is completely redrawn, Figures 2–3 are rearranged vertically, and tables and prompt boxes are reformatted. v2 adds Tables 2, 3, and 5 and Figures 6–7; the earlier example tables become Tables 6–7.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for IFEval, ComplexBench, and BFCL while retaining the earlier related-work coverage. Section 4.4.2 further positions SimpleToolHalluBench as detecting a failure mode missed by instruction-following and conventional tool-calling benchmarks.

T1.justification: Section 5.2 changes the formal discrimination-score definition from raw classification accuracy to accuracy minus 0.5 and defines zero as chance-level performance. The principal CKA, GRPO, and DPO mathematics is retained, although v2's Appendix C.1 introduces an unexplained extra pi_ref symbol in the displayed probability ratio.

improvement.justification: The new RL-without-reasoning control and independent instruction-following/tool-competence checks address an important weakness in v1's attribution of hallucination to reasoning (Tables 2–3). Broader model validation, benchmark-screening details, and explicit causal limitations further strengthen the paper. Strong causal language remains in places, and new Figures 6–7 contain caption/legend inconsistencies, limiting the mechanistic additions. Nevertheless, the central behavioral evidence is substantially better controlled and supported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe The Reasoning Trap and retain the same benchmark and central experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison. Renumbered and relocated material can be matched; some new appendix captions conflict with their plots, but this does not prevent comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds reasoning ablations, instruction-following and tool-calling evaluations, additional model comparisons, and appendix CKA analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original SynTool and GSM8K training experiments, model evaluations, representation analyses, and mitigation results in Figures 2–5 and Tables 1–2.

results.title: The Reasoning Trap: How Enhancing LLM Reasoning Amplifies Tool Hallucination

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on router-aware stabilization demonstrated on Countdown and mathematics. v2 adds the diagnosis of routing drift, volatile mismatch signals and clipping activity preceding collapse as an explicit central contribution, and extends its effectiveness claims to code benchmarks.

C2.justification: The basic explanation linking router drift, importance-ratio variability and clipping already appears in v1. v2 refines its temporal interpretation, describes entropy as an indicator of policy collapse rather than expert diversity, and adds quantified throughput and memory tradeoffs in Section 5.6.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly specifies layer/expert counts, rollout group size, exact clipping ranges, the default router-shift floor, reward verifiers and code evaluation details. Section 5.6 documents caching costs. Conversely, v2 removes v1's PyTorch snippet, small-model parameter counts, pretraining learning rate, eight-H100 hardware statement and verl implementation disclosure.

E1.justification: Countdown and the five mathematics benchmarks are retained. v2 adds code training using PrimeIntellect, LeetCode, TACO and LiveCodeBench, with evaluation on LiveCodeBench, MBPP and HumanEval, substantially extending task and domain coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains Base, GRPO, GSPO and GMPO. The corresponding plug-in comparison expands from GRPO/GSPO with and without router shift in v1 Figure 4 to include GMPO with and without router shift in v2 Figure 4. The freezing and replay comparators remain in Appendix D.

E3.justification: v1 specifies a global batch size of 128 across experiments; v2 Appendix A.1 reports 256 for the small-scale setting and retains 128 at large scale. Countdown plots cover longer horizons and report training reward instead of the earlier validation trajectories. Added code protocols include 32K-token generation and LiveCodeBench v4–v5 evaluation with training data described as preceding v5.

E4.justification: v2 adds comparative routing-severity, importance-ratio and clipping diagnostics in Figure 5, efficiency analysis in Section 5.6, and expanded plug-in stability testing. Floor sensitivity, stop-gradient and freezing/replay analyses already appeared in v1; their appendix placement does not establish new experiments.

E5.justification: v2 Sections 5.1–5.2 newly report means over three random seeds for training curves and results. Both versions specify 32 repeated AIME24 evaluations. This adds seed-count disclosure without establishing an increase in runs; no confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is added.

E6.justification: All mathematics values in Table 1 are retained, including RSPO's 77.1 average. Added code results give RSPO an 85.2 average versus GMPO's 82.5. v2 also adds or revises reward, entropy and diagnostic trajectories, reports a 20.8% throughput reduction relative to GMPO, and estimates approximately 1.5 GiB of routing-cache memory.

M1.justification: v1 Section 3.2 and Equation (5) apply router-shift weighting after token-level clipping. v2 Section 4.2 and Equations (9)–(11) multiply the weight into the importance ratio before clipping and aggregation. This changes the central objective and clipping decisions. The router-shift statistic, flooring and stop-gradient already existed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries, method and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. v2 introduces a standalone diagnosis section and reorganizes technical details, baseline objectives and analyses into Appendices A–E. This substantially changes the document's explanatory structure.

P2.justification: Table 1 becomes a grouped mathematics/code table. v2 adds reward and mechanism-diagnostic plots, combines the plug-in comparisons, adds a stop-gradient plot and removes the router schematic. Existing floor and replay panels are separated and relocated, entropy is redrawn, and captions and page layouts change substantially.

R1.justification: The dedicated related-work discussion is largely retained. v2 adds Qin et al.'s Countdown-generation reference and removes the Omni-MATH, DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen2.5 technical-report references. It also more explicitly positions its main instantiation as GMPO plus router-shift weighting.

T1.justification: The formal update changes from post-clipping weighting in v1 Equation (5) to pre-clipping ratio rescaling in v2 Equation (11), and Equation (8) defines a router-shift clipping-fraction statistic. The underlying drift statistic is algebraically retained, and much baseline mathematics is reorganized. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The routing and clipping diagnostics substantially strengthen the empirical support for v1's largely inferential instability explanation. Code evaluation broadens validation, while explicit configurations, seed reporting and quantified overhead make the evidence and practical costs easier to assess. These gains outweigh the lost implementation snippet and pretraining details, although the relationship between the revised weighting order and unchanged mathematics scores remains unexplained.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RSPO research. Their text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v1 has no appendices; v2's Appendices A–E are complete and readable.

after.justification: v2 retains original Countdown and mathematics experiments and adds code benchmark results, training diagnostics and throughput measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original Countdown training and ablation experiments and Qwen3-30B-A3B mathematical reasoning results in Table 1 and Figures 2–5.

results.title: Towards Stable and Effective Reinforcement Learning for Mixture-of-Experts

C1.justification: The abstract and new Section 2.1 add silent-speech synthesis in ALS, operation with approximately 40 minutes of training data, and phoneme-guided synthesis as central contributions. V1's speculative few-shot/zero-shot potential statement disappears. The central claim linking EMG power to self-supervised speech representations remains.

C2.justification: New Section 7 acknowledges single-participant clinical evidence, untested day-to-day shifts, and absent long-term validation. Appendices B–D add interpretations of phonetic associations, data-limited learning, and EMG-to-text tradeoffs. V2 also explains how perceptually plausible synthesized speech can coexist with high linguistic error rates and qualifies cross-study performance comparisons.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents transcript-derived gTTS targets, the separate use of recorded audio for probing, channel normalization, detailed TDS architecture, loss weights, and the 50-epoch AdamW schedule. It supplies code/data/project links and states resource release, replacing v1's future-availability footnote. These are substantial disclosure gains; unspecified v1 details do not establish underlying procedure changes.

E1.justification: V2 retains the healthy speech and 12-participant gesture datasets under explicit names and adds DATA_ALS: approximately one hour of silent articulation from an ALS participant, covering 600 sentences and roughly 300 words. Appendix D.4 adds word-level EMG-to-text evaluation and uses LibriSpeech-100 transcripts to construct its decoder.

E2.justification: The main covariance, diagonal-power, and spectrogram comparators remain. Appendix D.4/Table 6 adds an evaluated EMG2TEXT alternative to direct EMG2SPEECH. Section 5.2 omits v1's audio-spectrogram-to-EMG-spectrogram probe, reported at r = 0.37. Appendix C's expanded literature comparisons are contextual citations rather than newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The healthy corpus's reported training/validation/test split changes from 7000/1000/1660 to 8500/760/400 sentences. V2 adds the ALS split of 500/40/60, human transcription by three raters across all 460 test utterances, MOS evaluation by ten raters on 35 utterances, and training-size experiments with fixed validation/test splits.

E4.justification: V2 adds CTC-only versus phoneme-guided training comparisons, analysis of unit-to-phoneme associations (Figure 6), a training-size ablation (Figure 7), training/validation loss analysis (Figure 8), and human transcription error distributions (Figure 9). These substantially extend the retained feature comparisons and layer-wise probes.

E5.justification: V1 Tables 1–2 already contain plus/minus values without specifying seed counts. V2 Tables 1–4 explicitly report averages over five random seeds, and Table 3 adds p < 10^-6 for phoneme-guided training. V2 also reports cross-rater variability. The PDFs do not establish an increase from a known previous run count.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 contain replacement results under the revised split: full-covariance UER changes from 58.7% to 56.08%, and PER from 41.42% to 32.78%. Gesture-power clustering accuracy changes from 70.6% to 61.41%, with chance corrected from 10% to 7.69%. New results include phoneme-guided UERs of 51.81%/46.98%, human WERs of 62.55%/50.82% for healthy/ALS data, and MOS 3.79.

M1.justification: V1 lists phoneme-guided decoding as future work. V2 Section 5.3.1 and Appendix B implement dual CTC prediction heads, a GRU-derived unit-to-phoneme probability table, and a consistency loss. Appendix D.4 also introduces an EMG-to-text pipeline using a pronunciation lexicon, language model, and WFST decoder.

P1.justification: V2 extensively revises prose and reorganizes existing material: gesture acquisition moves into Data, recording details move to Appendix A, and Continuing Work is replaced by Conclusion and Limitations. It adds a contributions subsection and separate dataset/result subsections, changes SS terminology to S3, and renames the rotation-invariance module shift-tolerant.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Existing figures are resized and renumbered, with electrode photographs moved to Appendix A. Tables 1–2 gain feature-dimension columns, while new Tables 3–6 and Figures 6–10 present the additional comparisons and analyses. Correlation-figure captions also clarify the quantities compared.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix C substantially expand positioning against earlier EMG and invasive speech interfaces, including Benster et al. (2024), with detailed distinctions concerning alignment, vocabularies, streaming, and evaluation comparability. Additional references support longitudinal stability, covariance geometry, language-model decoding, and perceptual evaluation.

T1.justification: Appendix B introduces mathematical definitions for the unit-conditioned phoneme table, posterior marginalization, consistency loss, and combined training objective. The existing covariance geometry and linear-probing formulation remain substantively unchanged. The additions formalize the new method without introducing theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1 left phoneme-guided decoding and assessment of generated audio as continuing work. V2 implements that method, adds full-test-set human intelligibility evaluation and sampled MOS ratings, demonstrates silent articulation in ALS, and substantially improves implementation and access documentation. These additions resolve important gaps in validating and reproducing the synthesis claim. High WER, one ALS participant, and revised data splits still limit clinical and cross-version performance conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe emg2speech and retain identifiable methods and experiments. All pages, equations, figures, and tables are readable. V1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–D, which were included in the comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds ALS decoding, phoneme-guided training, human intelligibility and quality ratings, and additional empirical analyses in the appendices.

before.justification: Sections 5.1–5.3 report original gesture-clustering results, speech-representation correlations, and unit and phoneme decoding experiments.

results.title: emg2speech: synthesizing speech from electromyography using self-supervised speech models

C1.justification: V2 adds an explicit new-probe contribution and extends the main claims to ordinal information and activation steering. Its introduction strengthens v1's error-tracing account into a claim that sinusoidality determines arithmetic accuracy, while the conclusion centers the necessity of specialized interpretability tools. The underlying universality claim is retained.

C2.justification: V2 interprets improved output decoding as challenging prior gradual-refinement accounts and develops stronger arguments about misleading general-purpose probes. New limitations address English-centric models, three-family coverage, exclusion of models above 30B parameters, and a suspected zero-index blind spot. Appendix A.8 also newly qualifies layer removal because correct lower-layer predictions are scarce.

D1.justification: New Appendix B documents initialization, regularization, optimizers, learning rates, dimensions, training steps, checkpoint selection, and steering optimization, substantially expanding v1's sparse implementation account. These are largely new disclosures, not demonstrated changes to old settings. Conversely, v1's explicit description of uniform number replacement for balancing natural-language contexts is omitted.

E1.justification: Section 4.3 adds decoding of weekday names, month names, and written numerals from 'one' to 'ten', extending the evaluated task beyond digit-valued number representations. The original eight natural-language datasets across four domains and the BBC multi-token-number setting remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds lin, bin, and log comparators to the arithmetic output-decoding experiments, where v1 examined sinusoidal probing (v2 Figure 7 versus v1 Section 4.2). The prior sin probe also becomes the explicit comparator in the new steering and ordinal experiments. The earlier TunedLens comparison is retained.

E3.justification: The Figure 3a probe comparison changes from synthetic arithmetic contexts to natural-language contexts, and Figure 5b expands held-out-layer evaluation from three to six models. New protocols include leave-one-out ordinal validation and steering incorrect predictions with an interpolation factor optimized per layer, operation, and probe. Newly disclosed hyperparameters alone do not establish changes to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds a mechanistic intervention study comparing activation steering across layers and probe types (Figure 9), plus an error analysis reporting that temporal decoding failures persist at the first position when token order is reversed. V1's layer-removal, sparsity, and transformer-component analyses remain in Appendices A.6–A.8.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a defined uncertainty-estimation procedure. The added leave-one-out evaluation changes validation design rather than introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds output-probe results, steering that corrects up to 30% of multiplication errors and 42% of division errors under optimized settings, and ordinal results including 11/12 month names decoded by param-sin across six models. Input, cross-layer, and conditional output-recovery plots also change alongside the new probe and settings. These are not straightforward same-setting gains over v1; Table 2's earlier results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: V2 introduces param-sin, assigning each latent feature a sine wave with learnable frequency, phase, and amplitude, beyond v1's inherited sinusoidal-basis probe (Section 3.2, Equation 2). It also adds target-conditioned activation steering using optimized patch embeddings and interpolation; v1's intervention removes layers.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around universality and specialized probing tools. V2 adds an explicit contribution list, reframes Section 4, moves several mechanistic analyses into the appendices, and adds Limitations, Experimental Details, and an LLM-use disclosure. Author and affiliation information also changes.

P2.justification: V2 changes the main layout from one column to two, reorganizes existing figures, and moves several displays into the appendices. It adds output-comparison and steering figures, an ordinal-results table, and a non-number Fourier-spectrum display. Figures 3 and 5 gain new series, and Figure 4's caption clarifies the color and line-style meanings.

R1.justification: V1 primarily extends Kadlcik et al.'s probe; v2 positions its own architecture against that probe's generalization limitations and explicitly challenges Zhou et al.'s gradual-refinement interpretation. It adds connections to Engels et al. on ordinal representations and Mickus et al. on embedding structure, while removing broader motivation references such as Kalai et al. This substantially revises the contribution's positioning.

T1.justification: Equation 2 adds a mathematical definition of the parameterized sinusoidal probe and its single-sine-wave constraint. The revision does not add formal theorems or proofs; its principal new mechanistic support is experimental.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central probing evidence through explicit output-baseline comparisons, targeted interventions, and ordinal generalization tests. Appendix B addresses v1's sparse implementation documentation, while new limitations clarify applicability. These gains improve the paper's assessability and reproducibility. The stronger causal wording still needs qualification: steering uses known correct targets and optimized interpolation, so its reported benefits do not establish a generally deployable error-correction method.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work despite the changed title and substantial revision. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching analyses moved into v2's appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical analyses and adds experiments with a new probe, activation steering, and ordinal-data decoding.

before.justification: V1 reports original representation-similarity measurements, probing experiments, cross-layer and cross-context evaluations, and arithmetic layer-removal results.

results.title: Language Models Learn Universal Representations of Numbers and Here’s Why You Should Care

C1.justification: The abstract replaces consistent superiority over existing reweighting methods with strongest overall average performance, emphasizing lower-capacity models. The introduction similarly narrows the performance contribution. The central optimization-based reweighting and improved RL-initialization contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses failures to outperform baselines when models already reason strongly or supervision mismatches the target task. It adds explanations for declining performance with larger training sets and for simple-task degradation, softens the RL-ceiling interpretation, and limits the AdamW analysis to a local approximation. Appendix I also introduces a mechanism interpretation involving more exploratory, self-corrective reasoning.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies probing-batch size 32 and practical loss-ratio scaling in Algorithm 1, corrects the forward-pass accounting, and documents parallel probing, GPU configurations, and measured step times. It also supplies settings for the added SGD/DAPO experiments and a planned code-release address. These expand implementation and resource documentation; the PDF does not establish that code has been released.

E1.justification: The math/code training corpora, BigMath RL data, and evaluation tasks are retained, including GSM8K and MATH500. Added models, optimizer comparisons, and computational experiments reuse existing task coverage rather than introducing new datasets, domains, or input scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds GRPO and DAPO as direct competitors to VCORE in Appendix F and Table 11, extending comparisons beyond SFT reweighting approaches. v1 uses GRPO only for downstream training of DFT/VCORE initializations and merely cites DAPO. Existing comparator sets in retained experiments remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce Qwen3-1.7B and Mistral-7B configurations, batch sizes 16/64, learning rates 1e-5/1e-4, plain SGD without momentum or weight decay, and probing-batch/hardware variations. The direct RL comparison also introduces a DAPO protocol with filtering disabled. Retained training, inference, and downstream RL settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds learning-rate/batch-size sensitivity tests (Table 3), probing-size and computational scheduling trade-offs (Appendix G), optimizer robustness (H.2), and qualitative CoT case studies (I). These substantially expand the existing data-size, reweighting-hyperparameter, and loss-scaling analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions specify seed 42 for main training and inference. Neither reports repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: The original results in Table 1 and v1 Tables 2–3, retained as v2 Tables 4–5, are numerically unchanged. v2 adds substantial new results in Tables 2–3 and 11–14. For example, Table 11 reports AIME accuracy of 40.00/43.33/48.33 for GRPO/DAPO/VCORE; Table 13 adds SGD averages of 38.69/38.14/40.11 for SFT/DFT/VCORE. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements to retained scores.

M1.justification: The core Gibbs reweighting and variance-scaling pipeline remains. Appendix H.1 adds an optimizer-aligned extension using Jacobian-adjusted token utilities and probing directions, extending v1's SGD formulation. This does not establish that the implementation underlying the retained main results changed.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify the abstract, preliminary motivation, method explanation, and experimental observations. Acknowledgments are added, and existing appendices are renumbered around new material. The original main-section order and most retained exposition remain, rather than undergoing wholesale restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adds six tables and the computational execution diagram in Figure 5. Table 1 gains shaded average columns and includes the Original model in best/second-best highlighting. Existing figures and tables are retained and reflowed around these substantial display additions.

R1.justification: v2 adds Gema et al. and Stechly et al. to contextualize CoT failures, and removes the distinct high-entropy-token study by Wang et al. and exploration study by Vassoyan et al. Section 4.1 instead emphasizes confidence- and importance-based comparators. The broader related-work organization and research positioning remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorem 1 and its proof concerning strict first-order improvement over uniform weighting. Appendix H.1 additionally develops a local Adam/AdamW extension with explicit assumptions, approximation bounds, optimizer-aligned utilities, an unbiased probing derivation, and an explicit Adam Jacobian. These go substantially beyond v1's derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through direct RL comparisons, optimizer and hyperparameter checks, and measured computational overhead, while narrowing the headline superiority claim to better match the unchanged main results. These substantially improve assessment of effectiveness and practicality. The gains are qualified: repeated-run uncertainty remains absent, and Appendix A's assertion of a finite Gibbs temperature for every positive KL budget overlooks saturation cases.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VCORE research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, revised, and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds model comparisons, robustness experiments, computational measurements, and qualitative reasoning examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning experiments, benchmark accuracies, and analyses of training-set size, reweighting hyperparameters, and loss scaling.

results.title: VCORE: Variance-Controlled Optimization-based Reweighting for Chain-of-Thought Supervision

C1.justification: The central claims of competitive accuracy, much smaller models, efficiency, and transparency remain. v1's explicit headline claim of greater interpretability is narrowed in v2 to insights obtained from inspecting embeddings, rather than retained as a principal comparative advantage.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning greater GEMS–LLM error complementarity on unseen questions, message-passing advantages over classical baselines, affordable ensembling, and diminishing returns from larger prompted LLMs. Most existing limitations remain. However, the Setting 3 discussion drops v1's explicit acknowledgment that GEMS does not outperform few-shot fine-tuning.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new baselines' per-question one-hot inputs and factorization objective, and specifies probability averaging for the ensemble. Appendix C.3 corrects the stated expected-performance subgroup count from 11 to 10 while retaining the listed bins. Existing GEMS hyperparameters, hardware information, prompts, and code-access information are largely unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate OpinionQA, Twin-2K, and Dunning–Kruger responses under missing-response, new-individual, and new-question settings. The added comparisons and analyses use this existing coverage; the change from discrete-choice to close-ended terminology does not introduce a different task.

E2.justification: v2 adds XGBoost in Settings 1–2 and matrix factorization in Setting 1 across all three datasets (Table 5). It also adds GPT-5-Mini, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 3 Flash prompting comparisons on OpinionQA (Table 9). Qwen2.5-7B, evaluated in v1 Table 5, is removed from the corresponding extended comparison in v2 Table 8.

E3.justification: v2 introduces paired-correctness evaluation of the best GEMS and LLM methods across three OpinionQA settings, plus an 11-model ensemble evaluation. The existing individual-level and question-level splits, accuracy metric, edge masking, and main training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds error-overlap analysis (Table 4), classical controls examining the contribution of graph structure (Table 5), and an ensemble study testing whether inexpensive repeated training improves accuracy (Table 6). The earlier LoRA-capacity, hidden-layer, and projection-pair ablations are retained in Appendix F.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies 11 different model initializations for the ensemble. This is ensemble construction, not an increase in uncertainty-estimation runs for the existing results. Tables 1–3 retain the same three-split mean-and-standard-deviation reporting, and the LoRA ablation remains explicitly single-seed.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 are numerically unchanged, but v2 adds classical-baseline, proprietary-model, error-overlap, and ensemble results. For example, Gemini 3 Flash reaches 52.78% with 8-shot Agentic CoT on OpinionQA Setting 1, while the new GEMS ensemble reaches 51.65% in Setting 3 versus 50.13% for the retained single-model result. Extended-table values are also corrected: Mistral-7B zero-shot accuracy changes from 35.60 in v1 Table 5 to 34.63 in v2 Table 8, matching Table 1; this does not establish a same-setting performance change from rerunning experiments.

M1.justification: The graph construction, encoders, decoder, losses, and LLM-to-GNN projection remain unchanged. v2 adds an inference variant that averages predicted probabilities from 11 differently initialized GEMS models (Section 6, Table 6).

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, extensively rewrites the abstract and introduction, replaces much discrete-choice terminology with close-ended simulation, and restructures the narrative. Related work moves before the problem definition, while limitations and ethical considerations move from Appendix A into main-text Sections 8–9.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, substantially reflowing equations, tables, and prompt examples. v2 adds Tables 4–6 and 9 and restructures the extended LLM table. The original three-panel compute figure is retained as appendix Figure 4, alongside a revised Setting 1 display in main-text Figure 3.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including Bianchi et al. and Zhou et al. on open-ended simulation and Lakshminarayanan et al. on ensembles, while removing works including Tang et al. and the Qwen2.5 report. Its positioning between LLM simulation, graph recommendation, and classical discrete-choice modeling remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: The graph definitions, mathematical objectives, and encoder/decoder equations are retained. Changes such as replacing the GraphSAGE root-transformation symbol with the self-transformation symbol are not substantive mathematical revisions. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important comparative gap in v1 by adding learned classical baselines, allowing readers to assess whether graph modeling offers value beyond simpler non-language methods. Four proprietary-LLM comparisons, error-overlap analysis, and measured ensemble gains substantially strengthen the evidence supporting the paper's central argument; corrected extended-table scores also improve consistency. The added comparisons still provide limited uncertainty and implementation detail, and the Setting 3 discussion is less explicit about trailing fine-tuning, but the overall evidential improvement is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GEMS research, despite a changed title and document format. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original classical-baseline comparisons, proprietary-LLM evaluations, error analysis, and ensemble results.

before.justification: v1 reports original GEMS and baseline experiments across three datasets and settings in Tables 1–3, with additional evaluations and ablations in the appendices.

results.title: Graph-Based Alternatives to LLMs for Human Simulation

C1.justification: Both versions claim an automated black-box framework that learns reusable strategies from successful, partial, and failed attacks, using three strategy libraries. The central claims of superior attack effectiveness, query efficiency, and strategy transferability remain. Revised numerical summaries and additional supporting experiments do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds reward-shaping and sparse-feedback interpretations, explains why abstracted strategies outperform raw logs, and interprets the new defense, judge, and redundancy analyses. It also introduces substantive qualifications about internal computation, latency, token consumption, and strategy-library initialization, alongside an argument about amortized costs in Appendix C.6.

D1.justification: V2 names embedding alternatives and documents additional component configurations and token accounting. Algorithm 1 corrects the judge input from the attack prompt to the target response, aligning it with the existing prose. However, v1's explicit 1024-dimensional embedding specification, zero target-temperature statement, and retrieval threshold are omitted. Baseline recipes, system prompts, and code-on-request access remain.

E1.justification: HarmBench's 400 queries and AdvBench-50 remain the datasets. V2 adds defended-target scenarios involving paraphrasing, perplexity filtering, and external safety classifiers in Section 4.5. Changes to the evaluated LLM configurations are addressed under E3.

E2.justification: The six main attack baselines remain PAIR, TAP, GPTFuzzer, ReNeLLM, CipherChat, and CodeAttack. V2 adds a defense comparison against an undefended control using Paraphrase, Perplexity Filter, Llama Guard 3, and OpenAI Moderation in Table 5. The latest-model comparison uses existing attack baselines.

E3.justification: The main evaluation replaces Qwen3-8B and GPT-4o-mini with DeepSeek-R1; Appendix C.2 adds GPT-5.1, Gemini-3-Flash, and Qwen3-max. New protocols include retrieval-count sweeps, embedding and component-model substitutions, validation on 700 attack-response pairs, and judge-agreement and token-cost metrics. The main ten-query budget and ASR/AQ definitions are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds binary-scoring and raw-interaction-log ablations, retrieval-count sensitivity, defense tests, embedding and weaker-component analyses, alternative-judge validation, redundancy analysis, and token-cost analysis. It also expands strategy examples and adds a case study. V1's w/o ALL results match v2's w/o Retrieval results exactly; those values are retained evidence rather than a new ablation result.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeat counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's alternative-judge agreement percentages add validation outcomes, rather than uncertainty estimates or repeated-run reporting.

M1.justification: The core architecture, three strategy libraries, and prompts match. However, v1 specifies a similarity threshold of 0.50 plus three retrieved strategies per library; v2 retains three per library but omits the threshold. Sections 3.4 and 4.1 do not establish whether the gate was actually removed or merely omitted from the description.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites and condenses the abstract, introduction, related work, methodology, and results narrative. It introduces a Formulation subsection, moves Algorithm 1 into Appendix A and ethical considerations before the references, adds a separate Limitations section, and reorganizes the appendices.

P2.justification: V2 substantially changes the document format, redraws Figures 1-2, transposes and expands Table 4, and revises the target columns in the main tables. Figures 5-7 and Tables 5-12 add new visual material, including sensitivity plots, a workflow diagram, and supplementary comparisons.

R1.justification: V2 adds JailbreakRadar, recent jailbreak studies by Yan et al. and Zheng et al., and sources for the evaluated defenses. It removes several references associated with v1's web-focused introduction, including PagedAttention, WebGPT, and Toolformer. The central positioning around continuous strategy accumulation remains.

T1.justification: V2 introduces Section 3.1 and an explicit optimization objective defining the optimal strategy through maximization of the judge's scalar score. This adds a limited mathematical formulation to v1's procedural description. No theorems, proofs, or theoretical guarantees are added.

improvement.justification: V2 fills an important validation gap by directly testing graded scoring and strategy extraction, which v1 supported mainly through library ablations. Alternative-judge validation, defense tests, and explicit computational limitations substantially strengthen the evidence and qualification of the central claims. Reproducibility concerns remain: the retrieval threshold is unexplained, and Table 7 reports PAIR query averages above the stated ten-query budget. These issues limit some added evidence but do not outweigh the stronger component validation and clearer efficiency tradeoffs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ASTRA and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. The retained framework and experiments can be matched despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds component ablations, defense evaluations, and appendix analyses of judges, embeddings, redundancy, and token costs.

before.justification: V1 reports original HarmBench and AdvBench-50 experiments, including attack success rates, query counts, transfer tests, and library ablations.

results.title: ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs

C1.justification: V2 adds explicit core contributions concerning quantitative ICL hallucination assessment and dependency-based formalization-difficulty assessment. Its abstract, introduction, and conclusion also emphasize DDR as a plug-and-play component for both SFT and ICL formalizers, broadening the contribution beyond v1's retrieval and RA-centered performance claims.

C2.justification: V2 distinguishes hallucination-free retrieval from relevant retrieval and develops dependency statistics into an alternative difficulty indicator. Diff01 is explicitly excluded because imprecise descriptions defeat that indicator, extending v1's discussion of ICL versus SFT behavior. New limitations concern special constructs such as MOD and maintenance across library versions; the existing abbreviated-name and missing-metadata limitation remains.

D1.justification: New Appendix D supplies detailed dependency-retrieval and dependency-conditioned formalization prompts with examples. Appendix C adds exact model identifiers for Claude, GPT-4o, and Qwen-Max. Training hyperparameters and the dataset-access address are retained, while v1's explicit instruction to fill missing RA metadata fields with None is omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions use FineLeanCorpus for Lean 4 dependency retrieval and statement autoformalization, retaining Diff01 through Diff89 and the MMA-trained baseline. The added analyses and model configurations use the existing data and task coverage.

E2.justification: V1's retrieval comparison contains R@5, R@10, and DDR. V2 adds five prompt-based LLM retrievers to that comparison and evaluates no retrieval, prompt-based retrieval, and DDR within each general LLM in Table 5. These substantially expand comparator participation beyond the retained SFT baselines.

E3.justification: The reported retrieval-matching rule changes from component-suffix matching to substring plus component-sublist matching. V2 explicitly evaluates retrieval after hallucination filtering, drops F1, adds hallucination-rate evaluation and three-way retrieval controls, and replaces first-success distributions with intermediate pass@k curves. V2 specifies @8 for its autoformalization tables; v1 describes both @1 and @8 without identifying Table 3's budget.

E4.justification: V2 adds a quantitative hallucination study and weighted dependency-based difficulty analysis. V1's RA-focused multi-attempt analyses are replaced by comparisons across general LLMs: DeepSeek-R1 appears in the main text, with four additional models and repeated DeepSeek panels in Appendix A. The Diff01 examples themselves are retained.

E5.justification: V1 Figure 3 reports across-sample standard deviations for precision, recall, and F1; that reporting disappears. V2 instead reports hallucination-rate means and standard deviations in Table 2. Both retain eight generation attempts, without establishing additional training runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance testing.

E6.justification: Many results are replaced: RA+DDR's Diff45 TypeC/BEq entries change from 0.60/0.59 in v1 Table 3 to 0.930/0.255 in v2 Table 4. Retrieval scores also change and F1 entries disappear. New results include ICL hallucination means of 0.21–0.39 versus 0.00–0.02 for DDR, plus the expanded LLM comparisons. Protocol and budget-reporting differences prevent interpreting the replacements as established same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The Qwen3-32B fine-tuning, dependency-name generation, suffix-array verification, and dependency-conditioned formalization pipeline are retained. Suffix Array Check names the existing verification procedure; the new integrations do not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten, and parts of the methodology are condensed. Detailed setup moves into Appendix C, the discussion is redistributed between results and a dedicated Limitations section, and the appendices are reorganized and expanded.

P2.justification: V2 transposes and expands the retrieval table, separates SFT and ICL results, adds a hallucination table, removes the retrieval-dispersion figure, and replaces the multi-attempt displays with new curves and appendix grids. Figures 1–2 and the examples are retained with relocation or caption changes. Typography and page layout also change throughout.

R1.justification: V2 adds the GPT-4o system card and Qwen2 technical report. The related-work survey and principal contrast with selection-based retrieval largely persist, with additional positioning around hallucination assessment and alternatives to LLM difficulty graders.

T1.justification: V2 revises the identifier-match relation in Appendix C and introduces the explicit definition of hallucination rate in Section 4.3. These are limited mathematical-definition changes. The suffix-array construction and search-complexity reasoning remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V1 tests DDR retrieval chiefly against R@5/R@10 and downstream integration with RA. V2 adds generative-retrieval comparators, controlled retrieval-strategy comparisons within five LLMs, and direct hallucination measurements, substantially strengthening evidence for DDR's usefulness beyond that setup. Prompt disclosure and specific limitations improve transparency. Retrieval-dispersion reporting is lost and cross-version score replacements remain insufficiently explained, but the stronger controlled evaluation provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Direct Dependency Retrieval study. Their complete texts, tables, figures, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: V2 reports original hallucination, retrieval, and autoformalization results in Tables 2–5, with further multi-attempt results in Appendix A.

before.justification: V1 reports original dependency-retrieval and autoformalization experiments in Tables 2–3, with retrieval dispersion and multi-attempt analyses in Figures 3–5.

results.title: Improving Autoformalization Using Direct Dependency Retrieval

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the contribution from demonstrated mathematical-reasoning gains to non-math generalization, explicitly claiming 3.9% relative improvement on reasoning and program-synthesis tasks. They also foreground negligible overhead. The original three methodological contributions and 3.0% relative math-improvement claim remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting embedding-score correlations to reward-shaping robustness and execution success to reliable tool use. It explicitly acknowledges runtime success as a proxy that cannot establish logical correctness, and adds a qualitative overhead rationale. Table 4 also corrects gamma=1's interpretation from disabling turn-level rewards to disabling discounting.

D1.justification: v2 adds procedural pseudocode in Algorithm 1, documents global normalization and zero-positive handling, and identifies additional embedding models with access links. Appendix A.3 describes one embedding per trajectory and a rough seconds-level cost. Original hyperparameters and evaluation-setting disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: Section 6.2 adds GPQA Diamond, BBEH-mini, and EvalPlus HumanEval/MBPP evaluations, substantially extending coverage beyond mathematical reasoning to non-math reasoning and program synthesis. The five original math benchmarks and training datasets remain. Removing OlympiadBench from Table 2's caption corrects an unsupported listing rather than removing reported results.

E2.justification: v2 Table 5 adds evaluated DAPO and SimpleTIR comparators on MATH 500 and AIME 2024 under the ablation training budget. This substantially broadens the trained-method comparison beyond GRPO. The original prompting and GRPO baselines remain; v1's conceptual DAPO comparison was not an empirical evaluation.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, EvalPlus testing, a three-embedding correlation protocol, and runtime-success rate as a tool-quality metric. These substantially broaden the evaluation design. Existing numerical training and evaluation settings in Section 5.1 and v1 Appendix A.2, retained as v2 A.4, remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Sections 6.3–6.4 add analyses testing whether code-similarity scores agree across embedding models and whether increased tool use accompanies executable code. These address robustness and tool errors beyond the original analyses. Existing component, discount, reward-shaping, and turn-count ablations remain, including the reward-shaping analysis relocated to Appendix A.5.

E5.justification: Section 6.3 newly introduces Pearson and Spearman correlation estimation for embedding-based similarity scores, reported in Table 8. Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the statistical addition does not quantify uncertainty in performance gains.

E6.justification: Original math scores and ablation values are retained, including v1 Tables 5–6 as v2 Tables 10–11. New Tables 5–9 add substantial results: Llama averages are 21.18 for GRPO versus 23.01 for GTPO, and non-math averages are 46.1 versus 47.9. Tool-execution success improves on average, but GTPO scores lower on AMC23: 69.49 versus GRPO's 72.17.

M1.justification: Equation 7 changes the specified advantage normalization from normalization across trajectories at a fixed turn to pooling all turns across sampled trajectories, also reflected in Algorithm 1. This revises one calculation within the retained three-component GTPO design; it does not establish that experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the core narrative remain. v2 updates the title and affiliations, shortens parts of Related Work and Background, clarifies notation, adds a Discussion section and appendix explanations, and moves the reward-shaping discussion into the appendix. Rewriting of retained material is localized.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the conceptual comparison table and substantially expands experimental displays through Tables 5–9 and a full-width Algorithm 1. Several existing figures and tables are relocated, including the reward-shaping table becoming Appendix Table 10. All eight original figures retain their graphical content.

R1.justification: The redesigned Table 1 and new Appendix A.1 substantially expand positioning against GRPO/DAPO/GSPO and ReTool/ToRL/Search-R1, including an explicit first-formulation claim for the combined design. New benchmark and temporal-credit-assignment citations are added, while the SFT-related discussion and several associated references are removed.

T1.justification: Equation 7 substantively revises the mathematical normalization set to include all trajectory-turn pairs. Section 4.3 also specifies the previously undefined no-positive-sample case. The turn-level MDP and discounted-return formulation remain, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the earlier paper's narrow empirical validation through matched DAPO/SimpleTIR comparisons, another model family, and four non-math benchmarks (Tables 5–7). The revised normalization specification and pseudocode also improve methodological clarity. These gains outweigh limitations in the additions: embedding correlations do not directly establish training robustness, overhead remains qualitatively argued, and Table 9's claim of consistent improvement contradicts its AMC23 result.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GTPO research work. Their complete main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched reliably despite additions and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, another model family, non-math evaluations, embedding correlations, and tool-execution analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original mathematical-reasoning evaluations, component ablations, training curves, and generated-code case studies in Section 5 and the appendix.

results.title: Empowering Multi-Turn Tool-Integrated Agentic Reasoning with Group Turn Policy Optimization

C1.justification: The central claim of extending SAM3 to instructions while preserving concept grounding remains. However, v3's abstract, introduction, and conclusion elevate HMPL-Instruct into a unified benchmark contribution covering object/part targets and one-to-one, one-to-many, and one-to-all grounding. This substantially expands v1's stated data contribution and incorporates capabilities previously described as future directions.

C2.justification: v3 interprets subset-grounding results as evidence against category-level overfitting and adds explanations of contrastive weighting, concept anchoring, and adapter specialization. Its limitations retain cardinality bias but add the absence of dense grounded understanding and conversational capabilities. v1's specific adaptive-routing/MoE and broader ReasonSeg evaluation outlooks are removed.

D1.justification: Appendices B and D add detailed annotation workflows, point-to-mask assignment, JSON export information, adapter insertion sites, bottleneck dimension 64, 1024-dimensional four-head attention, and approximately 311.9M trainable parameters. v3 also specifies rho, margin, and temperature settings and explicitly states dataset availability alongside code. The existing hardware and batch-size disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: PACO-LVIS-Instruct evolves into HMPL-Instruct with explicit part-level annotations and one-to-many subset grounding, including 2,941 subset samples, substantially expanding v1's reported object-level dataset. v3 also evaluates RefCOCO and Ref-ZOM in Table 4; these were not evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: The main SAM3 comparison drops the Qwen3-VL-2B agent variant while retaining the 8B variant under the shortened SAM3 Agent name. v3 adds LISA and UniPixel to HMPL-Instruct comparisons in Tables 3 and 8, and evaluates LISA, ReLA, UniPixel, and SAM3 Agent on the external benchmarks in Table 4.

E3.justification: The ablation protocol expands from component removal in v1 Table 2 to stagewise training, individual-loss additions, and a single-adapter control in v3 Table 5, with explicit rho and margin sweeps in Appendix C.
